questions.q: Which textbook by William Stallings, in its 8th edition, is the primary course text for data and computer communications?
o: Data and Computer Communications
Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach
Data Communications and Networking
Computer Networks
questions.e: The main course text is 'Data and Computer Communications' by William Stallings, 8th Edition. The reference text is 'Data Communications and Networks' by Achyut S. Godbole, a separate work.

questions.q: In the general communication model, which element encodes information so as to produce transmittable signals, with a modem given as the example?
o: Destination
Source
Transmitter
Receiver
questions.e: The transmitter encodes information to produce signals suitable for transmission, and a modem is the classic example. The source merely generates the data to be sent, with telephones and PCs as its examples.

questions.q: In the five-element communication model, what is the correct order of components from origin to endpoint?
o: Source, transmission system, transmitter, receiver, destination
Source, transmitter, transmission system, receiver, destination
Transmitter, source, transmission system, destination, receiver
Source, receiver, transmission system, transmitter, destination
questions.e: The model runs source, transmitter, transmission system, receiver, destination. The transmission system connects source side to destination side and may be a single line or a complex network such as IP or the PSTN.

questions.q: A network confined to a room, building or campus, a network spanning a city, and a network spread across a country or the globe are respectively called:
o: WAN, MAN, LAN
MAN, LAN, WAN
LAN, WAN, MAN
LAN, MAN, WAN
questions.e: A small geographical area such as a room, building or campus is a LAN, a city-wide network is a MAN, and a network spread across a country or the globe is a WAN. The distinction is purely one of geographic scope.

questions.q: Distributed processing, given as an application of networks, is exemplified by which technology?
o: Remote computing
Instant messaging
GRID computing
Message broadcast
questions.e: GRID computing is cited as the example of distributed processing among network applications. Message broadcast and remote computing are listed separately under the communication category of applications.

questions.q: A connection in which a dedicated link is provided between exactly two devices is called:
o: Multipoint
Multicast
Point-to-point
Broadcast
questions.e: A point-to-point connection provides a dedicated link between two devices. A multipoint connection is the alternative, in which more than two specific devices share a single link.

questions.q: Network topology is defined as describing which of the following?
o: The rules governing how data is formatted and acknowledged
The maximum data rate supported by the physical medium
The layout of the wire and devices, and the paths used by data transmissions
The addressing scheme used to identify hosts
questions.e: Topology defines the way computers, printers and other devices are connected, describing both the layout of wire and devices and the paths used by data transmissions. Formatting and acknowledgement rules are the domain of protocols instead.

questions.q: In which topology does every device have a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device?
o: Bus
Star
Mesh
Ring
questions.e: Mesh topology gives every device a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device, with each link carrying traffic only between the two devices it connects. This is why it is robust and secure but requires far more cable and ports, making it expensive.

questions.q: Which topology's principal disadvantage is that it constitutes a single point of failure?
o: Bus
Mesh
Star
Ring
questions.e: Star topology connects every device by a dedicated point-to-point link to a central controller, usually a hub, so failure of that hub is a single point of failure. Its advantages are lower expense, ease of installation and reconfiguration, and robustness of the individual links.

questions.q: In bus topology, what is a 'drop line'?
o: A connection running between a device and the main cable
A connector that punctures the cable sheathing to contact the metallic core
A backup cable used when the backbone fails
The terminating resistor at each end of the backbone
questions.e: A drop line is the connection running between a device and the main cable. A tap is the different component: a connector that either splices into the main cable or punctures the sheathing to make contact with the metallic core.

questions.q: Which topology is described as a multipoint topology in which all devices are linked through a backbone cable?
o: Bus
Ring
Star
Mesh
questions.e: Bus topology is the multipoint arrangement where all devices connect to a backbone cable via drop lines and taps. Its ease of installation is offset by difficult reconnection and fault isolation, and a break in the bus cable stops all transmission.

questions.q: In ring topology, what component must each device incorporate?
o: A repeater
A tap
A hub
A bridge
questions.e: Each device in a ring incorporates a repeater, because the signal is passed device to device around the ring until it reaches its destination. Its stated disadvantage is that traffic is unidirectional.

questions.q: Tree topology is described as integrating which combination of topologies?
o: Multiple star topologies onto a bus
Multiple mesh topologies onto a star
Multiple bus topologies onto a ring
Multiple ring topologies onto a mesh
questions.e: Tree topology integrates multiple topologies together, with the given example being multiple star topologies joined onto a bus. Its key vulnerability is that if the backbone line breaks, the entire segment goes down.

questions.q: Which is listed as a disadvantage of tree topology?
o: The overall length of each segment is limited by the type of cabling used
There is no support from hardware and software vendors
Every device requires a dedicated link to every other device
Traffic can only travel in one direction
questions.e: The overall length of each segment in a tree topology is limited by the cabling type, and the arrangement is more difficult to configure and wire than other topologies. Vendor support is actually listed as an advantage, alongside point-to-point wiring for individual segments.

questions.q: Which five items make up the listed network components?
o: Topology, protocol, addressing, routing, switching
Routers, switches, hubs, cables, servers
Source, transmitter, medium, receiver, destination
Physical media, interconnecting devices, computers, networking software, applications
questions.e: The network components are physical media, interconnecting devices, computers, networking software and applications. The source-to-destination list belongs instead to the general communication model.

questions.q: Networking media is defined as which of the following?
o: The set of devices that regenerate and forward signals
The physical layout describing how devices are connected
The means by which signals are sent from one computer to another, by cable or wireless
The software that governs how devices exchange messages
questions.e: Networking media is the means by which signals or data are sent from one computer to another, either by cable or by wireless means. The physical layout of devices is topology, a separate concept.

questions.q: In a client/server network arrangement, what characterises the server?
o: It shares its resources only when idle
It alternates between requesting and serving depending on load
It is a dedicated computer whose only function is to respond to client requests
It operates purely at the physical layer
questions.e: In a client/server arrangement, network services are located in a dedicated computer whose only function is responding to client requests. That server centrally holds file, print, application, security and other services and remains continuously available.

questions.q: Data communication is defined specifically as which of the following?
o: The physical layout of devices and cabling
The exchange of information in any form between any two parties
The routing of packets between different networks
The exchange of data between two computers or data devices
questions.e: Communication is the general exchange of information, whereas data communication is narrowed to the exchange of data between two computers or data devices, dealing with transmitting signals reliably and efficiently. Networking is the third related term, covering the technology and architecture used to interconnect communicating devices.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an application running over computer networks?
o: Cyclic redundancy checking
Frequency division multiplexing
Internet telephony (VoIP)
Bit stuffing
questions.e: Internet telephony (VoIP) is listed among network applications alongside e-mail, searchable web data, e-commerce, news groups, video conferencing, chat groups, instant messengers and Internet radio. Multiplexing, CRC and bit stuffing are underlying transmission and link-layer techniques rather than user-facing applications.

questions.q: A hybrid topology given as an example combines which arrangement?
o: A bus backbone with three ring networks
A ring backbone with three mesh networks
A mesh backbone with three star networks
A star backbone with three bus networks
questions.e: The hybrid example presented is a star backbone with three bus networks attached. Hybrid arrangements exist because real installations rarely fit a single pure topology.

questions.q: A protocol is defined as a set of rules and conventions between sender and receiver. Which three key features characterise it?
o: Encoding, modulation and multiplexing
Addressing, routing and switching
Syntax, semantics and timing
Framing, sequencing and acknowledgement
questions.e: The three key features of a protocol are syntax, semantics and timing. Syntax covers what is communicated, semantics covers how it is interpreted, and timing covers when it should be communicated.

questions.q: A rule stating that the first 16 bits of a message always contain the receiver address is an example of which protocol feature?
o: Syntax
Flow control
Timing
Semantics
questions.e: Syntax concerns the structure or format of data, so a rule fixing which bit positions carry the address is syntactic. Semantics would instead govern interpretation, such as a rule that an address ending in '00' means sender and receiver are on the same network.

questions.q: A rule that the sender must wait after sending 1000 bytes for an acknowledgement is an example of which protocol feature?
o: Encapsulation
Semantics
Syntax
Timing
questions.e: Timing covers data transmission rate and duration, including when a sender must pause and wait for an acknowledgement. Syntax and semantics concern the format and the interpretation of the data respectively, not its scheduling.

questions.q: In a protocol architecture, what is the relationship between adjacent layers?
o: Each layer relies on the next lower layer for more primitive functions and provides services to the next higher layer
Each layer duplicates the functions of the layer below for redundancy
Layers operate independently with no service relationship
Each layer communicates only with the topmost layer
questions.e: A protocol architecture divides a large task into smaller subtasks, with each layer relying on the next lower layer for more primitive functions and providing services to the next higher layer. The lower layer also conceals its details from the upper layer, which is what makes layers substitutable.

questions.q: Standards that arise by convention rather than by legislation are classified as which type?
o: Statutory
De facto
Regulatory
De jure
questions.e: De facto standards arise by convention, while de jure standards come about by regulation and are legislated by an official body. De facto standards subdivide further into proprietary and non-proprietary.

questions.q: Within de facto standards, what distinguishes a proprietary standard from a non-proprietary one?
o: Proprietary is open and free to implement; non-proprietary requires licensing
Proprietary is legislated by government; non-proprietary is not
Proprietary is closed, invented and owned by an organization; non-proprietary is open, developed by an organization, committee or group that vendors then support
Proprietary applies only to hardware; non-proprietary only to software
questions.e: Proprietary de facto standards are closed, invented and owned by an organization, and became popular on their own; non-proprietary ones are open, developed by an organization, committee or group that became popular with vendors then supporting them. Legislation by an official body is the mark of de jure standards, not of either de facto subtype.

questions.q: Why are standards introduced in the first place?
o: To assign addresses uniquely across the Internet
To increase the data rate of transmission media
To make services and goods compatible with other vendors and manufacturers
To reduce the cost of network hardware
questions.e: Standards exist to make services and goods compatible across different vendors and manufacturers. Compatibility, not performance or cost, is the stated motivation.

questions.q: An intranet, accessible only to people inside a company and not readily sharing data with outside systems, is an example of which kind of system?
o: Closed system
Open system
Distributed system
Federated system
questions.e: A closed system does not connect easily with other systems and may be restricted to certain devices or a limited group, with a company intranet as the example. The Internet is the contrasting open-system example, since any computer or phone can connect and exchange data using common protocols.

questions.q: Which organization is categorised as a standards creation committee rather than a forum or a regulatory agency?
o: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineering (IEEE)
Internet Society (ISOC)
ATM Forum
Federal Communication Commission (FCC)
questions.e: IEEE is a standards creation committee, alongside ISO, ITU-T (formerly CCITT), ANSI and EIA. ISOC and the ATM Forum are forums formed by user groups, students, industry representatives and experts, while the FCC is a government-appointed regulatory agency.

questions.q: Which pair of bodies are the regulatory agencies named among standards organizations?
o: IETF and ISOC
IEEE and ANSI
ITU-T and EIA
FCC and PTA
questions.e: The Federal Communication Commission and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority are the named regulatory agencies, defined as government-appointed bodies. IETF and ISOC are forums, while IEEE, ANSI, ITU-T and EIA are standards creation committees.

questions.q: Which standards body is identified as having formerly been known as CCITT?
o: ANSI
ITU-T
EIA
ISO
questions.e: The International Telecommunication Union-Telecom Standards Section (ITU-T) is the body formerly known as CCITT. ISO is the International Standards Organization, a separate committee.

questions.q: How many layers does the OSI reference model define?
o: Six
Four
Seven
Five
questions.e: The OSI model has seven layers, dividing network communication into distinct layers each responsible for specific tasks. The TCP/IP suite is the model with five layers in its modern presentation and four in its original definition.

questions.q: In the seven-layer OSI model, which layers relate to communications technology as opposed to user applications?
o: Layers 1-3 relate to communications technology; layers 4-7 relate to user applications
Layers 1-4 relate to communications technology; layers 5-7 relate to user applications
Layers 1-5 relate to communications technology; layers 6-7 relate to user applications
Layers 1-2 relate to communications technology; layers 3-7 relate to user applications
questions.e: Layers 1 through 4 relate to communications technology and layers 5 through 7 relate to user applications. The boundary falls just above the transport layer, which is also where the communications subnet boundary is drawn.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles encryption and compression, translating data into a format the application layer can understand?
o: Presentation layer
Application layer
Transport layer
Session layer
questions.e: The presentation layer translates data into a format the application layer can understand and handles encryption and compression, with SSL/TLS encryption, JPEG and MP4 given as examples. The session layer instead starts, manages and ends the dialogue between two devices.

questions.q: Managing and controlling the dialogue between computers — starting, maintaining and ending communication — is the responsibility of which OSI layer?
o: Transport layer
Session layer
Network layer
Presentation layer
questions.e: The session layer manages the dialogue or session between computers, analogous to making a phone call: it starts the call, keeps the conversation going and ends it. Logging into online services and session management in web browsers are its example applications.

questions.q: Which OSI layer ensures data is delivered without errors and in the correct order, managing flow control and retransmission, with TCP and UDP as its example protocols?
o: Network layer
Session layer
Data link layer
Transport layer
questions.e: The transport layer ensures error-free, correctly ordered delivery and manages flow control and retransmission, with TCP and UDP as its named protocols. The network layer sits below it and is concerned instead with routing data between different networks.

questions.q: IP addresses, routers and the Internet Protocol are given as the applications of which OSI layer?
o: Transport layer
Data link layer
Physical layer
Network layer
questions.e: IP addresses, routers and the Internet Protocol belong to the network layer, which manages routing between different networks and decides the best path. MAC addresses, switches and network interface cards belong one layer lower, at the data link layer.

questions.q: Which OSI layer organizes data into frames and handles error detection and correction, with MAC addresses and switches as its applications?
o: Physical layer
Network layer
Data link layer
Transport layer
questions.e: The data link layer organizes data into frames and handles error detection and correction, using MAC addresses, switches and network interface cards. The physical layer below it deals only with the physical connection itself — cables, fiber optics and Wi-Fi signals.

questions.q: In the email scenario used to illustrate the OSI model, at which layer is the message broken into smaller packets with TCP ensuring they arrive in order?
o: Layer 5, session
Layer 3, network
Layer 4, transport
Layer 6, presentation
questions.e: Breaking the email into smaller packets and using TCP to ensure ordered arrival happens at layer 4, the transport layer. Layer 3 then gives each packet the destination IP address and routes it across networks.

questions.q: In OSI terminology, what are entities in the same layer on different machines called?
o: Peer entities
Service access points
Protocol data units
Adjacent entities
questions.e: Active elements in a layer are called entities, and entities occupying the same layer on different machines are peer entities. Each layer provides services to the layer above it and consumes services from the layer below.

questions.q: Connection-oriented and connectionless services are compared to which everyday systems respectively?
o: The telephone system and the railway system
The telephone system and the postal system
The railway system and the postal system
The postal system and the telephone system
questions.e: Connection-oriented service is likened to the telephone system, where a connection is established before communication, while connectionless service is likened to the postal system, where each item is sent independently. Each service also carries an associated quality of service, such as reliable or unreliable.

questions.q: Which application is given as typically requiring a reliable service, and which as typically not requiring one?
o: Both file transfer and voice traffic require reliability
File transfer requires reliability; voice traffic does not
Neither file transfer nor voice traffic requires reliability
Voice traffic requires reliability; file transfer does not
questions.e: File transfer is the typical application for a reliable service, while voice traffic typically does not need one. Reliable services never lose or corrupt data but cost more, so the trade-off is made per application.

questions.q: In the layered analogy where two friends exchange letters, a translator machine converts between a language and a secret code. Which layer does the translator occupy in the three-layer version?
o: Layer 3
Layer 2
It sits outside the layered model
Layer 1
questions.e: In the three-layer version the friends themselves are layer 3 producing the letter in their own language, the translator machines are layer 2 converting to and from the secret code, and the post office is layer 1 carrying the physical envelope. In the earlier face-to-face version, communication happened in a single layer using signs.

questions.q: In an exchange using the OSI model, what happens to the data as it descends the sending stack?
o: Each layer removes a header before passing data down
Each layer adds a header, with the data link layer also adding a trailer
Headers are added only at the application and transport layers
Only the physical layer adds control information
questions.e: Descending the stack, each layer adds its own header to the data unit, and the data link layer adds both a header and a trailer before the bit stream is placed on the transmission medium. The receiving stack reverses this, stripping each layer's control information on the way up.

questions.q: The OSI model is best characterised as which of the following?
o: A routing protocol used across the Internet backbone
An internationally standardised conceptual model for open systems that communicate with other systems
A proprietary architecture owned by a single vendor
A physical wiring specification for local area networks
questions.e: OSI is an internationally standardised conceptual reference model dealing with open systems, meaning systems open for communication with other systems. It serves as a reference guide for understanding and designing network architecture rather than as a deployed protocol stack.

questions.q: The original TCP/IP protocol suite was defined as how many software layers built upon the hardware?
o: Four
Three
Seven
Five
questions.e: The original TCP/IP suite was defined as four software layers built upon the hardware: Application, Transport, Internet and Network Interface. Today it is commonly presented as a five-layer model with names matching the OSI layers.

questions.q: In the modern five-layer presentation of TCP/IP, the original 'Internet' and 'Network Interface' layers correspond respectively to which layers?
o: Transport and Network
Network and Physical
Network and Data Link
Data Link and Physical
questions.e: The original Internet layer corresponds to the Network layer (layer 3) and the original Network Interface layer corresponds to the Data Link layer (layer 2). The original suite's 'Hardware Devices' maps to the Physical layer, which the four-layer version did not count as a software layer.

questions.q: When the OSI model and the TCP/IP suite are compared side by side, which OSI layers are absorbed into the single TCP/IP application layer?
o: Application, presentation and session
Application and presentation only
Session and transport
Presentation, session and transport
questions.e: The TCP/IP application layer spans the OSI application, presentation and session layers, containing several application protocols. Transport, network, data link and physical map across one-to-one between the two models.

questions.q: Which was developed first, and what is the consequence for their layer structures?
o: OSI was developed first, and TCP/IP layers match it exactly
They were developed simultaneously with identical layers
TCP/IP was developed prior to the OSI model, and its layers do not match OSI exactly
OSI was developed first, and TCP/IP deliberately used fewer layers to match
questions.e: The TCP/IP protocol suite was developed prior to the OSI model, which is why its layers do not match the OSI layers exactly. The mismatch is historical rather than by design.

questions.q: What is stated as the major difference between the OSI model and TCP/IP?
o: OSI is a conceptual model not practically used for communication, whereas TCP/IP is used for establishing connections and communicating
TCP/IP is conceptual while OSI is deployed in practice
OSI supports routing while TCP/IP does not
OSI is faster but TCP/IP is more secure
questions.e: The major difference is that OSI is a conceptual model that is not practically used for communication, whereas TCP/IP is actually used to establish connections and communicate over the network. Both remain the two most widely used networking models for describing communication.

questions.q: HTTPS, SSL and SFTP are given as examples of which category of network protocol?
o: Network routing protocols
Network security protocols
Network management protocols
Network communication protocols
questions.e: HTTPS, SSL and SFTP are network security protocols, which implement security over network communications. Basic data communication protocols such as TCP/IP and HTTP form the communication category, while SNMP and ICMP are management protocols.

questions.q: SNMP and ICMP are classified as which type of protocol?
o: Network communication protocols
Network management protocols
Network security protocols
Application transfer protocols
questions.e: SNMP and ICMP are network management protocols, providing network governance and maintenance. TCP/IP and HTTP are the examples given for basic network communication protocols.

questions.q: In the postal-system analogy for TCP/IP, what plays the role of the postal offices through which mail is routed?
o: Web servers
Packets
Routers
IP addresses
questions.e: In the analogy, routers correspond to the postal offices through which mail is routed, IP addresses correspond to the sender and recipient information, and packets correspond to the individual envelopes. Retransmission of lost or damaged parts completes the analogy.

questions.q: HTTP is described as operating at what level relative to TCP/IP, and governing what?
o: Below the transport layer, handling packet fragmentation
At the same level, providing an alternative to IP addressing
At a lower level, governing physical signalling
At a higher level, specifying how web browsers and web servers communicate to request and transmit web content
questions.e: HTTP operates at a higher level than TCP/IP and specifies how web browsers and web servers communicate to request and transmit web content such as pages, images and videos. The library analogy casts the browser as a borrower, the server as a librarian, and the URL as the book title requested.

questions.q: Which TCP/IP application provides remote login capability, allowing a user to emulate a terminal on a remote system?
o: Telnet
SMTP
FTP
HTTP
questions.e: Telnet provides remote login, letting a user emulate a terminal on a remote system. SMTP handles basic e-mail transfer between hosts, and FTP sends files from one system to another on user command.

questions.q: SMTP is described as providing which facility?
o: Mapping domain names to addresses
Remote terminal emulation
Basic e-mail facility, transferring messages among hosts
Transferring files on user command
questions.e: SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, provides the basic e-mail facility by transferring messages among hosts. File transfer on user command is FTP's role.

questions.q: Encapsulation is defined as the addition of control information to data. Which three kinds of control information are listed?
o: Address information, error-detecting code and protocol control
Source port, destination port and window size
Sequence number, timestamp and checksum
Preamble, postamble and flag
questions.e: Encapsulation adds address information, an error-detecting code and protocol control to the data. This is why a transport protocol data unit gains a transport header and a network protocol data unit gains a network header as data descends the stack.

questions.q: Splitting larger data blocks into smaller ones is called segmentation in general terms. What is the equivalent term in TCP/IP?
o: Reassembly
Fragmentation
Encapsulation
Multiplexing
questions.e: The process is called segmentation generally and fragmentation in TCP/IP. It is needed because application layer messages may be large while network packets are bounded in size.

questions.q: What are the stated block sizes for ATM cells and Ethernet frames?
o: ATM cells are 64 octets; Ethernet frames are up to 1024 octets
ATM cells are 53 octets; Ethernet frames are up to 1526 octets
ATM cells are 53 octets; Ethernet frames are up to 512 octets
ATM cells are 48 octets; Ethernet frames are up to 1500 octets
questions.e: ATM blocks, called cells, are 53 octets long, while Ethernet blocks, called frames, are up to 1526 octets long. The large difference in bounded block size is why segmentation is needed when data crosses between such technologies.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as an advantage of fragmentation?
o: Fewer interrupts at the receiver
Reduced processing time
More efficient error control and shorter delays
Reduced protocol overhead
questions.e: Fragmentation gives more efficient error control, more equitable access to network facilities, shorter delays and smaller buffer requirements. Its disadvantages are the opposite of the other options: increased overhead, more interrupts at the receiver and more processing time.

questions.q: Sequence numbers in connection control are used for which set of purposes?
o: Addressing, encapsulation and multiplexing
Encryption, compression and authentication
Fragmentation, reassembly and routing
Ordered delivery, flow control, error control and congestion control
questions.e: Sequence numbers support ordered delivery, flow control, error control and congestion control. Connection control itself spans establishment, data transfer and termination, with possible interruption and recovery.

questions.q: Flow control is performed by which entity, and using which mechanisms?
o: The physical layer, using signal amplification
The sending entity, using fragmentation and reassembly
The receiving entity, using stop and wait or credit systems such as sliding window
The network layer, using routing tables
questions.e: Flow control is done by the receiving entity to limit the amount or rate of data, using stop and wait or credit systems such as a sliding window. It is needed at the application layer as well as at the network layers.

questions.q: In the error control procedure described, what does the receiver do when it detects an error in a packet?
o: Forwards the packet unchanged to the application
Acknowledges the packet but flags it as damaged
Discards the packet, so that the absence of an acknowledgement triggers retransmission
Corrects the packet using the error-detecting bits and forwards it
questions.e: The sender inserts error-detecting bits and the receiver checks them, acknowledging if correct and discarding the packet if an error is found; the missing acknowledgement then causes retransmission after a timeout. Error detection bits allow errors to be found but not corrected in this scheme.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the characteristics of a networking model, alongside encapsulation and addressing?
o: Attenuation
Modulation
Multiplexing
Amplification
questions.e: Multiplexing is listed among the characteristics of a networking model, together with encapsulation, segmentation and reassembly, connection control, ordered delivery, flow control, error control, addressing and transmission services. Modulation, amplification and attenuation are physical transmission concepts rather than model characteristics.

questions.q: Why is a protocol architecture needed for data communications?
o: Because a single protocol cannot support more than one physical medium
Because network hardware vendors legally require layered designs
Because data communications requires complex procedures such as identifying the data path and receiver, negotiating preparedness at both system and application level, and translating file formats
Because encryption cannot function without layering
questions.e: A protocol architecture is needed because data communications requires complex procedures: the sender must identify the data path and receiver, the systems must negotiate preparedness, the applications must do likewise, and file formats may need translation. Achieving all of this demands a high level of cooperation, which layering organises.

questions.q: In the side-by-side comparison of the two models, what is noted about the network layer of the TCP/IP suite?
o: It contains the Internet Protocol and some helping protocols
It contains several application protocols
It contains several transport protocols
It is defined only by underlying LAN and WAN technology
questions.e: The TCP/IP network layer is described as containing the Internet Protocol together with some helping protocols. The data link and physical layers below it are characterised instead as underlying LAN and WAN technology, and the transport layer as holding several transport protocols.

questions.q: Twisted pair, coaxial cable and optical fiber are classified as which category of transmission media?
o: Direct media
Guided media
Multipoint media
Unguided media
questions.e: Twisted pair, coaxial cable and optical fiber are guided media. Unguided media are the contrasting category, exemplified by air, vacuum and seawater, where signals are not confined to a physical conductor.

questions.q: A direct link is defined as a transmission path with which property?
o: A path with at most one intermediate repeater
A path in which data flows in only one direction
A path that uses only guided media
A path between two devices with no intermediate devices, where signals propagate directly from transmitter to receiver
questions.e: A direct link is a transmission path between two devices with no intermediate devices, so signals propagate straight from transmitter to receiver. A direct connection between two computers using an Ethernet cable is the given example.

questions.q: A Wi-Fi network in a coffee shop where laptops, phones and tablets all connect to the same router illustrates which arrangement?
o: Direct link
Multipoint
Point-to-point
Simplex
questions.e: Multipoint means more than two devices share the same medium, which the coffee-shop Wi-Fi example illustrates. A direct Ethernet cable between two computers is the corresponding point-to-point example.

questions.q: Which transmission type allows both stations to transmit, but only one at a time, with a walkie-talkie as the example?
o: Multipoint
Half-duplex
Simplex
Full-duplex
questions.e: Half-duplex allows both stations to transmit but only one at a time, illustrated by a walkie-talkie. Full-duplex allows simultaneous transmission in both directions, illustrated by a telephone call, while simplex permits transmission in one direction only.

questions.q: A telephone call is given as the example of which transmission type?
o: Broadcast
Full-duplex
Simplex
Half-duplex
questions.e: A telephone call exemplifies full-duplex transmission, where both stations transmit simultaneously and signals are carried in both directions. The walkie-talkie is the half-duplex example, since only one party can speak at a time.

questions.q: Transmission impairments cause different consequences for analog and digital signals. What are they respectively?
o: Attenuation for analog; noise for digital
Bit errors for analog; degradation of signal quality for digital
Delay for analog; distortion for digital
Degradation of signal quality for analog; bit errors for digital
questions.e: Impairments cause degradation of signal quality in analog transmission and bit errors in digital transmission. The most significant impairments named are attenuation with attenuation distortion, delay distortion, and noise.

questions.q: Attenuation is defined as which phenomenon?
o: The pickup of a signal from one line by another
The gradual weakening or loss of signal strength as a signal travels through a medium
Unwanted random interference added to a signal
The arrival of different frequency components at different times
questions.e: Attenuation is the gradual weakening or loss of signal strength as the signal travels through a medium, with signal strength falling off with distance depending on the medium. Frequency components arriving at different times is delay distortion, a separate impairment.

questions.q: For a received signal to be usable, which two conditions on its strength must be satisfied?
o: It must exceed the modulation rate, and match the receiver's bandwidth
It must be constant across all frequencies, and free of any dc component
It must be below the medium's saturation level, and above the transmitter's output
It must be strong enough to be detected, and sufficiently higher than the noise to be received without error
questions.e: The received signal must be strong enough to be detected and sufficiently higher than the noise to be received without error. Amplifiers or repeaters are used to increase strength when these conditions would otherwise fail.

questions.q: Delay distortion arises because of which underlying cause?
o: Propagation velocity varying with frequency, so different frequency components arrive at different times
Multiple signals mixing and creating unintended new signals
The natural thermal movement of electrons in conductors
Signal strength falling off with distance
questions.e: Delay distortion occurs because propagation velocity varies with frequency, so various frequency components of a signal arrive at different times. It is particularly critical for digital data because parts of one bit spill over into others, causing inter-symbol interference.

questions.q: What is the specific consequence of delay distortion for digital data?
o: A permanent dc offset in the received signal
An increase in the modulation rate
Inter-symbol interference, as parts of one bit spill over into others
Complete loss of synchronization at the transmitter
questions.e: For digital data, delay distortion causes parts of one bit to spill over into adjacent bits, producing inter-symbol interference. This is why it is described as particularly critical for digital transmission.

questions.q: Which type of noise contains a mix of all frequencies and is compared to the constant hiss of an untuned radio channel?
o: Intermodulation noise
Thermal noise
Impulse noise
White noise
questions.e: White noise is named for containing a mix of all frequencies, much as white light contains all colours, and sounds like a constant hiss. It is constant and random with no distinct pattern, and is sometimes deliberately used to mask other sounds.

questions.q: Thermal noise arises from which physical cause, and how does it vary?
o: The mixing of nearby transmitted signals, increasing with signal count
The natural motion of electrons in conductors, increasing with temperature
Electromagnetic interference from outside, increasing with proximity
Coupling between adjacent signal paths, increasing with cable length
questions.e: Thermal noise results from the natural random motion of electrons in electrical conductors, and it increases as the temperature of the conductor rises. It is always present in any electronic system, which is why it sets a floor on achievable signal quality.

questions.q: Intermodulation noise is produced by which mechanism?
o: Random electron motion inside conductors
Short irregular pulses from external electromagnetic sources
Multiple signals interacting so as to create additional, unintended signals
A signal on one line being picked up by another line
questions.e: Intermodulation noise occurs when multiple signals transmitted through a system interact and create additional, unintended signals that were not originally present. It is more common in complex systems carrying many signals at closely spaced frequencies.

questions.q: Crosstalk is defined as which of the following?
o: The arrival of frequency components at different times
Irregular high-amplitude spikes of short duration
The weakening of a signal with distance
A signal from one line being picked up by another, through unwanted coupling between signal paths
questions.e: Crosstalk is a signal from one line being picked up by another as a result of unwanted coupling between signal paths. Irregular spikes of short duration and high amplitude describe impulse noise, a different category.

questions.q: Impulse noise is characterised by which combination of properties, and why is it especially damaging?
o: Long duration and low amplitude; it slowly erodes signal strength
Short duration and high amplitude; a single noise spike could corrupt many bits
Constant amplitude across all frequencies; it masks the entire signal
Frequency-dependent delay; it causes bits to overlap
questions.e: Impulse noise consists of irregular pulses or spikes of short duration and high amplitude, for example from external electromagnetic interference. It is a major source of error in digital data because one spike could corrupt many bits at once.

questions.q: In communication, a channel is defined as which of the following?
o: The medium or pathway through which information is transmitted from one point to another
The device that combines multiple signals into one
The set of rules governing data exchange
The maximum data rate achievable over a link
questions.e: A channel is the medium or pathway through which information travels from one point to another, likened to a road that vehicles travel on. It may be physical, such as wires, cables or air, or virtual, such as software or protocols used for transmission.

questions.q: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular networks are given as examples of which channel type?
o: Wireless channels
Wired channels
Unidirectional channels
Virtual channels
questions.e: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular networks are wireless channels, using radio waves, microwaves or infrared to transmit data through the air. Copper cables, fiber optic cables and coaxial cables are the wired examples.

questions.q: A TV broadcast and a phone conversation illustrate which contrast in channel direction?
o: Guided versus unguided
Analog versus digital
Unidirectional versus bidirectional
Narrowband versus broadband
questions.e: A TV broadcast is unidirectional, with data flowing in one direction only, while a phone conversation is bidirectional, with data flowing both ways. This is the direction-of-communication property of a channel, distinct from its physical medium.

questions.q: Channel capacity is described as a function of which set of factors?
o: Data rate, bandwidth, noise and error rate
Attenuation, crosstalk, latency and jitter
Modulation, encoding, framing and addressing
Voltage, current, resistance and power
questions.e: Channel capacity, the maximum possible data rate on a communication channel, is a function of data rate in bits per second, bandwidth in hertz, noise on the link and the error rate of corrupted bits, with limits imposed by physical properties. It is the ceiling on throughput rather than a measurement of any single one of these quantities.

questions.q: For a signal of bandwidth B, the Nyquist frequency is defined as what?
o: 2B
B
B squared
questions.e: For a bandwidth of span B, the Nyquist frequency is 2B, the minimum rate at which a finite-bandwidth signal must be sampled to retain all its information. Equivalently, given a bandwidth B, the highest signal rate that can be carried is 2B.

questions.q: The Nyquist formula for the capacity of a noiseless channel with M signal levels is:
o: C = B log2(1 + M)
C = B / (2 log2 M)
C = 2B log2 M
C = M log2 B
questions.e: The Nyquist formula is C = 2B log2 M, where B is bandwidth and M is the number of signal levels. For binary signals this reduces to 2B bps requiring bandwidth B Hz, and the rate can be raised by using more signal levels at the cost of receiver complexity.

questions.q: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 4000 Hz and transmits a signal with two signal levels. Using the Nyquist bit rate formula, what is the maximum bit rate?
o: 2000 bps
4000 bps
8000 bps
questions.e: Applying Bit Rate = 2 × Bandwidth × log2 L gives 2 × 4000 × log2 2 = 2 × 4000 × 1 = 8000 bps. With two levels each signal element carries one bit, so the rate is simply twice the bandwidth.

questions.q: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 4000 Hz and transmits a signal with four signal levels. What is the maximum bit rate?
o: 8000 bps
questions.e: Bit Rate = 2 × 4000 × log2 4 = 2 × 4000 × 2 = 16000 bps. Doubling the number of levels from two to four doubles the bit rate, because log2 4 is 2 rather than 1.

questions.q: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 20 kHz and must carry 280 kbps. How many signal levels are required?
questions.e: From 280 = 2 × 20 × log2 L, dividing gives 280/40 = 7 = log2 L, so L = 2^7 = 128 signal levels. The value 7 is the exponent, not the number of levels itself, which is the common trap in this calculation.

questions.q: The Shannon capacity formula for a noisy channel is:
o: C = 10 log10(B/SNR)
C = 2B log2 M
C = B log2(1 + SNR)
C = B × SNR
questions.e: Shannon capacity is C = B log2(1 + SNR), where B is the available bandwidth in hertz and SNR is the signal-to-noise ratio. It gives the maximum rate at which information can be reliably transmitted in the presence of noise, and practice falls below this theoretical maximum.

questions.q: The signal-to-noise ratio in decibels is computed as:
o: SNRdB = 10 log10(signal/noise)
SNRdB = log10(signal × noise)
SNRdB = 2 log2(signal/noise)
SNRdB = signal/noise × 100
questions.e: SNR in decibels is SNRdB = 10 log10(signal/noise), where SNR itself is average signal power divided by average noise power. Converting back the other way gives SNR = 10^(SNRdB/10).

questions.q: For an extremely noisy channel in which the signal-to-noise ratio is almost zero, what is the channel capacity?
o: Infinite
Equal to 2B
Zero
Equal to the bandwidth B
questions.e: Substituting SNR = 0 gives C = B log2(1 + 0) = B log2(1) = B × 0 = 0. The capacity collapses to zero because log2(1) is zero, meaning no information can be reliably transmitted when noise overwhelms the signal.

questions.q: A channel has a bandwidth of 3000 Hz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 3162. What is its approximate capacity?
o: About 3000 bps
About 11627 bps
About 66700 bps
About 34881 bps
questions.e: C = 3000 × log2(1 + 3162) = 3000 × log2(3163) = 3000 × 11.627 ≈ 34881 bps. The value 11.627 is the logarithm itself, not the capacity, so it must be multiplied by the bandwidth.

questions.q: If the signal-to-noise ratio of a channel is given as 36 dB, what is the corresponding linear SNR value?
o: Approximately 36000
Approximately 360
Approximately 3981
Approximately 3.6
questions.e: Rearranging SNRdB = 10 log10 SNR gives SNR = 10^(SNRdB/10) = 10^(36/10) = 10^3.6 ≈ 3981. This conversion from decibels to a linear ratio must be done before the value can be substituted into the Shannon formula.

questions.q: For a channel of bandwidth 10 kHz with an SNR of 20 dB, the Shannon capacity works out to approximately:
o: 20 kbps
66.7 kbps
100 kbps
10 kbps
questions.e: With B = 10,000 Hz and SNR = 10^(20/10) = 100, the capacity C = 10,000 × log2(101) ≈ 66,700 bps, or about 66.7 kbps. This is the maximum rate at which data can be sent while still maintaining reliable communication in the presence of that noise.

questions.q: Why does a faster data rate lead to higher error rates for a given noise level?
o: Because a faster rate shortens each bit, so a burst of noise affects more bits
Because faster rates reduce the number of signal levels available
Because faster rates increase the thermal noise in the conductor
Because higher rates require more bandwidth than is available
questions.e: A faster data rate shortens the duration of each bit, so a given burst of noise spans and corrupts more bits. This relationship between data rate, noise and error rate is what Shannon's formula captures via the signal-to-noise ratio.

questions.q: Bandwidth of a channel is defined as which of the following?
o: The ratio of signal power to noise power
The physical length of the transmission medium
The amount of data it can transmit in a given time period
The maximum number of devices that can share it
questions.e: Bandwidth refers to the amount of data a channel can transmit in a given period, so a wider bandwidth allows more data to be sent simultaneously and generally faster communication. Capacity is the related but distinct notion of the maximum amount of information the channel can carry, influenced by channel type and conditions such as interference and noise.

questions.q: Which four combinations of data type and signal type make up the set of encoding techniques?
o: ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM
Guided-unguided, wired-wireless, simplex-duplex and point-multipoint
NRZ, biphase, multilevel binary and scrambling
Digital-digital, analog-digital, digital-analog and analog-analog
questions.e: The four encoding technique categories are digital data with digital signal, analog data with digital signal, digital data with analog signal, and analog data with analog signal. NRZ, biphase and multilevel binary are specific schemes within the first of these categories.

questions.q: In signal encoding terminology, a scheme in which all signal elements have the same sign is called:
o: Pseudoternary
Unipolar
Bipolar
Polar
questions.e: Unipolar means all signal elements share the same sign. Polar is the contrasting term, where one logic state is represented by a positive voltage and the other by a negative voltage.

questions.q: Modulation rate is defined as the rate at which the signal level changes, and is measured in which unit?
o: Decibels
Hertz
Bits per second
Baud, meaning signal elements per second
questions.e: Modulation rate is measured in baud, meaning signal elements per second. Data rate is the separate quantity measured in bits per second, and the two differ whenever a signal element carries more or fewer than one bit.

questions.q: In encoding terminology, what do the terms 'mark' and 'space' denote?
o: Binary 1 and binary 0 respectively
The start and stop bits of a character
The beginning and end of a frame
A positive and a zero voltage level
questions.e: Mark and space denote binary 1 and binary 0 respectively. They are signalling terms rather than framing terms, so they are unrelated to start and stop bits.

questions.q: Why is the absence of a dc component desirable in an encoding scheme?
o: It eliminates the need for synchronization
It allows ac coupling via a transformer, whereas a dc component requires direct physical attachment of transmission components
It doubles the achievable data rate
It removes the need for any error detection
questions.e: With no dc component, ac coupling via a transformer becomes possible, whereas a dc component requires direct physical attachment of transmission components. Reduced high frequency content is a separate spectral advantage, since it lowers bandwidth requirements.

questions.q: Where should transmitted power ideally be concentrated within the transmission bandwidth, and why?
o: Near the lower band edge, because attenuation is lowest there
Spread evenly, because all frequencies behave identically
Near the upper band edge, because noise is lowest there
In the middle of the transmission bandwidth, because channel transmission characteristics are worse near the band edges
questions.e: Transmitted power should be concentrated in the middle of the transmission bandwidth because a channel's transmission characteristics are worse near the band edges. This is one of the signal spectrum criteria used to compare encoding schemes.

questions.q: Clocking, as a criterion for comparing encoding schemes, refers to what, and how can it be achieved?
o: Alignment of frames within a multiplexed stream, achieved by framing bits
Detection of errors, achieved by parity bits
Measurement of the total transmission time of a frame, achieved by timestamping
Determination of the beginning and end of each bit, achieved by a clock lead or by embedding synchronization information within the encoded signal
questions.e: Clocking is the determination of the beginning and end of each bit, and synchronization can be achieved either by a clock lead synchronizing transmitter and receiver, or by providing synchronization information within the encoded signal itself. The second approach is what makes self-clocking codes such as Manchester attractive.

questions.q: Immunity to signal interference and noise in an encoding scheme is expressed in terms of which measure?
o: Power Usage Effectiveness
Bit Error Rate (BER)
Modulation rate
Signal-to-noise ratio
questions.e: Noise immunity performance of a code is expressed in terms of Bit Error Rate. Cost and complexity form a separate comparison criterion, since some codes require a signal rate greater than the data rate, which raises cost.

questions.q: In NRZ-L encoding as defined here, which voltage represents which bit?
o: The bit value is determined by a transition rather than a level
Zero is high voltage and one is low voltage
One is high voltage and zero is low voltage
Both zero and one use positive voltages of different magnitude
questions.e: In NRZ-L as defined here, zero is represented by high voltage and one by low voltage, with the voltage held constant during the bit interval and no return to zero. Determination by transition rather than level is the defining feature of NRZI instead.

questions.q: In Nonreturn to Zero Inverted (NRZI), how is data encoded?
o: By the presence or absence of a signal transition at the beginning of the bit time
By a transition in the middle of each bit period
By the absolute voltage level held during the bit
By alternating the polarity of successive pulses
questions.e: NRZI encodes data as the presence or absence of a signal transition at the beginning of the bit time: 0 means no transition at the start of the interval and 1 means a transition. This makes it an example of differential encoding.

questions.q: What is the principal advantage of differential encoding over level-based encoding?
o: It halves the required bandwidth
It guarantees a transition in every bit period
Detection of a transition is more reliable than detection of a level, and polarity can easily be lost in complex transmission layouts
It removes the need for any error detection
questions.e: Differential encoding represents data by changes rather than levels, and detecting a transition is more reliable than detecting an absolute level, especially since it is easy to lose the sense of polarity in complex transmission layouts. Guaranteeing a transition every bit period is a property of biphase codes such as Manchester, not of differential encoding generally.

questions.q: Which pair correctly states the pros and cons of NRZ?
o: Pros: guaranteed synchronization; Cons: poor bandwidth efficiency
Pros: self-clocking and no dc component; Cons: requires more bandwidth
Pros: easy error detection and low bandwidth; Cons: three voltage levels needed
Pros: easy to engineer and good use of bandwidth; Cons: dc component and lack of synchronization capability
questions.e: NRZ is easy to engineer and makes good use of bandwidth, but suffers a dc component and lacks synchronization capability, so it is not often used for signal transmission. Self-clocking with no dc component describes biphase codes, which pay for those benefits in bandwidth.

questions.q: In Bipolar-AMI encoding, how are binary zero and binary one represented?
o: Zero by a positive pulse and one by a negative pulse
Zero by no line signal, and one by positive or negative pulses that alternate in polarity
Zero by alternating pulses and one by absence of signal
Both by transitions at the middle of the bit period
questions.e: In Bipolar-AMI a zero is represented by no line signal, while a one is represented by a pulse that alternates in polarity between successive ones. Pseudoternary is the exact inverse, with one represented by absence of signal and zero by alternating positive and negative pulses.

questions.q: Which synchronization problem does Bipolar-AMI solve, and which does it leave unsolved?
o: It solves loss of sync on long strings of ones, but zeros remain a problem
It solves both, requiring no scrambling
It solves loss of sync on long strings of zeros, but ones remain a problem
It solves neither, but removes the dc component
questions.e: Bipolar-AMI avoids loss of synchronization during a long string of ones because those ones produce alternating pulses, but a long string of zeros still produces no line signal and remains a problem. This unsolved case is precisely why scrambling techniques such as B8ZS and HDB3 were introduced.

questions.q: Pseudoternary is described as having what advantage over Bipolar-AMI?
o: Lower bandwidth requirement
Better synchronization on long strings of zeros
No advantage or disadvantage over Bipolar-AMI
Built-in error correction
questions.e: Pseudoternary is stated to have no advantage or disadvantage over Bipolar-AMI; it simply reverses which bit value gets the alternating pulses. Both belong to the multilevel binary family.

questions.q: What is the efficiency trade-off of multilevel binary schemes compared with NRZ?
o: They are not as efficient, since each signal element still represents only one bit while the receiver must distinguish three levels
They are more efficient, since each element carries two bits
They are equally efficient but require less power
They are more efficient but cannot detect errors
questions.e: Multilevel binary is not as efficient as NRZ because each signal element still represents only one bit, yet the receiver must distinguish between three levels (+A, −A and 0). This costs approximately 3 dB more signal power for the same probability of bit error.

questions.q: In Manchester encoding, how are binary 1 and binary 0 represented?
o: 1 is a positive pulse and 0 is no signal
1 is a high-to-low transition and 0 is a low-to-high transition, both at the start of the bit period
1 is a low-to-high transition and 0 is a high-to-low transition, both in the middle of the bit period
1 is a transition at the beginning of the bit period and 0 is no transition
questions.e: In Manchester encoding there is a transition in the middle of every bit period, with 1 encoded as low to high and 0 as high to low. Differential Manchester also has a mid-bit transition but encodes the data by whether there is an additional transition at the start of the bit period.

questions.q: Which standard is named as using Manchester encoding?
o: IEEE 802.5
IEEE 802.3
ITU-T V.32
IEEE 802.11
questions.e: Manchester encoding is used by IEEE 802.3. Differential Manchester is the related biphase code, distinguished by encoding 0 as a transition at the beginning of the bit period and 1 as no transition there.

questions.q: In Differential Manchester encoding, how is binary 0 distinguished from binary 1?
o: 0 is low-to-high in mid-bit; 1 is high-to-low in mid-bit
0 has no mid-bit transition; 1 has a mid-bit transition
0 has no transition at the start; 1 has a transition at the beginning
0 has a transition at the beginning of the bit period; 1 has no transition at the start
questions.e: In Differential Manchester, 0 is encoded as a transition at the beginning of the bit period and 1 as no transition at the start; both bit values still carry the mid-bit transition used for clocking. Encoding by mid-bit direction instead is plain Manchester.

questions.q: What is the main disadvantage of biphase codes such as Manchester?
o: They cannot provide any error detection
They require three distinct voltage levels
They require at least one transition per bit time and possibly two, so the maximum modulation rate is twice that of NRZ and more bandwidth is needed
They introduce a large dc component
questions.e: Biphase codes need at least one and possibly two transitions per bit time, so their maximum modulation rate is twice that of NRZ and they require more bandwidth. Their compensating advantages are self-clocking synchronization on the mid-bit transition, no dc component, and error detection.

questions.q: Which set of properties correctly describes the advantages of biphase encoding?
o: Lower bandwidth, no transitions and simple engineering
Guaranteed zero modulation rate and no synchronization needed
Self-clocking synchronization on the mid-bit transition, no dc component and error detection
Three-level signalling, 3 dB power saving and higher efficiency
questions.e: Biphase codes provide synchronization from the guaranteed mid-bit transition (self-clocking), have no dc component, and offer error detection. The three-level signalling and its 3 dB power penalty belong to multilevel binary schemes such as Bipolar-AMI.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a scrambling technique in signal encoding?
o: To encrypt the data so it cannot be intercepted
To increase the number of signal levels used
To replace sequences that would produce a constant voltage with filling sequences that produce enough transitions to maintain synchronization
To compress the data before transmission
questions.e: Scrambling replaces sequences that would otherwise produce constant voltage with filling sequences that generate enough transitions to keep the receiver synchronized. Critically, it achieves this with no reduction in data rate, unlike simply inserting extra bits.

questions.q: Which of the following is a required property of the filling sequence used in scrambling?
o: It must be the same length as the original, with no dc component and no long sequences of zero-level line signal
It must be shorter than the original sequence to save bandwidth
It must be encrypted with a shared key
It must be transmitted at half the original data rate
questions.e: The filling sequence must be the same length as the original, produce no dc component, avoid long sequences of zero-level line signal, and be recognizable to the receiver so the original can be restored. It must also add error detection capability without reducing the data rate.

questions.q: B8ZS stands for which technique, and which encoding is it based on?
o: Bipolar With 8 Zeros Substitution, based on pseudoternary
Binary 8 Zero Suppression, based on NRZ-L
Bipolar With 8 Zeros Substitution, based on Bipolar-AMI
Biphase 8 Zero Signalling, based on Manchester
questions.e: B8ZS is Bipolar With 8 Zeros Substitution and is based on Bipolar-AMI. It addresses the one weakness AMI leaves open, namely loss of synchronization during long runs of zeros.

questions.q: In B8ZS, if an octet of all zeros occurs and the last voltage pulse preceding it was positive, what substitution is made?
questions.e: If the preceding pulse was positive, an all-zero octet is encoded as 000+-0-+; if the preceding pulse was negative, it is encoded as 000-+0+-. Each substitution deliberately creates two violations of the AMI alternation rule.

questions.q: Why does the B8ZS substitution deliberately create violations of the AMI code?
o: Because violations increase the data rate
Because violations reduce the required bandwidth
Because violations remove the need for error detection
Because violations are unlikely to occur as a result of noise, so the receiver can reliably detect and interpret them as an octet of all zeros
questions.e: The substitution causes two AMI violations, which are unlikely to arise from noise, so the receiver can recognise the pattern and interpret it as an octet of all zeros. Using an ordinarily-illegal pattern as a marker is what makes the substitution unambiguous.

questions.q: HDB3 stands for which technique, and what does it replace?
o: High-Density Bipolar-3 Zeros, replacing a string of eight zeros with two pulses
High-Density Bipolar-3 Zeros, replacing a string of three zeros with a single pulse
High-Density Biphase-3 Zeros, replacing every third zero with a transition
High-Density Bipolar-3 Zeros, replacing a string of four zeros with sequences containing one or two pulses
questions.e: HDB3 is High-Density Bipolar-3 Zeros and replaces a string of four zeros with sequences containing one or two pulses. B8ZS is the related technique that acts on strings of eight zeros instead.

questions.q: In HDB3, which two factors jointly determine the substitution pattern used?
o: The number of zeros in the entire frame and the parity bit
The position of the string within the octet and the signal level
The polarity of the preceding pulse and whether the number of bipolar pulses since the last substitution is odd or even
The data rate and the bandwidth of the channel
questions.e: The HDB3 substitution is chosen from a table indexed by the polarity of the preceding pulse and by whether the count of bipolar pulses (ones) since the last substitution is odd or even. This two-way dependency is what keeps the running dc level balanced.

questions.q: In HDB3, if the polarity of the preceding pulse is negative and the number of bipolar pulses since the last substitution is odd, which substitution is used?
questions.e: With a negative preceding pulse and an odd count of bipolar pulses since the last substitution, the substitution is 000-. If the count were even instead, the substitution would be +00+.

questions.q: In HDB3, if the polarity of the preceding pulse is positive and the number of bipolar pulses since the last substitution is even, which substitution is used?
questions.e: With a positive preceding pulse and an even count of bipolar pulses since the last substitution, the substitution is -00-. With an odd count and the same positive preceding polarity, it would instead be 000+.

questions.q: How many zeros trigger a substitution in B8ZS compared with HDB3?
o: Eight in B8ZS and four in HDB3
Three in B8ZS and eight in HDB3
Eight in both
Four in B8ZS and eight in HDB3
questions.e: B8ZS acts on an octet of eight zeros, while HDB3 acts on a string of four zeros. The number appearing in each name refers to the zero-run length each scheme targets.

questions.q: Both B8ZS and HDB3 are built on top of which base encoding scheme?
o: Manchester
Bipolar-AMI
Differential Manchester
NRZ-L
questions.e: Both B8ZS and HDB3 are based on Bipolar-AMI, extending it to handle long runs of zeros. They are usually compared alongside plain Bipolar-AMI to show how each treats the same bit stream differently.

questions.q: Which device converts digital data to an analog signal so it can be transmitted over an analog line?
o: A codec
A modem
A multiplexer
A repeater
questions.e: A modem converts digital data to an analog signal for transmission over an analog line, using ASK, FSK or PSK. A codec performs the opposite class of conversion, turning analog data into digital form.

questions.q: Modulation involves operating on which characteristics of a carrier signal?
o: Wavelength, polarity and duration
Bandwidth, data rate and power
Voltage, current and resistance
Amplitude, frequency and phase
questions.e: Modulation operates on one or more of the three carrier characteristics: amplitude, frequency and phase, giving rise to ASK, FSK and PSK for digital data. A carrier signal is one with a steady waveform of constant amplitude and frequency until information is added.

questions.q: In Amplitude Shift Keying, how are the two binary values usually distinguished?
o: By two different frequencies near the carrier frequency
By shifting the carrier phase by 180 degrees
By different amplitudes of the carrier, with one amplitude usually zero so the presence and absence of the carrier is used
By combining amplitude and phase variation simultaneously
questions.e: ASK represents values by different amplitudes of the carrier frequency, and usually one amplitude is zero, so the presence and absence of the carrier signals the two values. Using two frequencies instead is FSK, and shifting phase is PSK.

questions.q: What is stated about the error performance of binary FSK relative to ASK?
o: BFSK cannot be compared to ASK
BFSK and ASK have identical error performance
BFSK is more susceptible to error than ASK
BFSK is less susceptible to error than ASK
questions.e: Binary FSK is less susceptible to error than ASK. BFSK is the most common form of FSK, representing the two binary values by two different frequencies near the carrier frequency.

questions.q: What is the trade-off associated with Multiple FSK (MFSK)?
o: Less bandwidth efficient, but less prone to error
Neither more efficient nor more error-prone, but simpler to build
More bandwidth efficient and less prone to error
More bandwidth efficient, but more prone to error
questions.e: MFSK uses more than two frequencies so each signalling element represents more than one bit, making it more bandwidth efficient but more prone to error. This efficiency-versus-error trade-off recurs across all multilevel modulation schemes.

questions.q: In Binary PSK, a phase shift of 180 degrees is equivalent to what?
o: Removing the carrier entirely
Flipping the sine wave
Halving the carrier frequency
Doubling the carrier amplitude
questions.e: A phase shift of 180 degrees, or pi radians, is equivalent to flipping the sine wave. In binary PSK, two such phases represent the two binary digits.

questions.q: How does Differential PSK differ from ordinary PSK?
o: It combines phase shifting with frequency shifting
The phase is shifted relative to the previous signal element, with no reference signal used
It requires four phases rather than two
It uses amplitude rather than phase to carry data
questions.e: In Differential PSK the phase of the modulated signal is shifted relative to the previous signal element rather than against an absolute reference, so no reference signal is needed. If the data bit is 0 the phase continues unchanged, and if it is 1 the phase is reversed, in the same manner as NRZI inverting on 1.

questions.q: In QPSK (quadrature PSK), what are the phase shift increments and how many bits does each signal element carry?
o: Shifts of 45 degrees giving eight phases, carrying 3 bits per element
Shifts of 180 degrees, carrying 1 bit per element
Shifts of 90 degrees giving four different phases, carrying 2 bits per element
Shifts of 120 degrees giving three phases, carrying 1.5 bits per element
questions.e: QPSK uses shifts of 90 degrees, giving four different phases, so each signal element represents 2 bits. Multilevel PSK extends this further, using 8 or more phase angles with each phase potentially carrying more than one amplitude.

questions.q: Quadrature Amplitude Modulation is described as a combination of which two techniques?
o: PSK and PM
FSK and PSK
ASK and FSK
ASK and PSK
questions.e: QAM combines ASK and PSK, and is described as a logical extension of QPSK. It sends two different signals simultaneously on the same carrier frequency by using two copies of the carrier, one shifted by 90 degrees, each ASK modulated.

questions.q: In QAM, how are two independent signals carried over the same medium?
o: By alternating the two signals in successive time slots
By using two copies of the same carrier, one shifted by 90 degrees, each ASK modulated
By using two different carrier frequencies
By assigning each signal a distinct spreading code
questions.e: QAM uses two copies of the carrier, one shifted by 90 degrees, each independently ASK modulated, so two independent signals travel over the same medium and are demodulated and combined to recover the original binary output. Using separate time slots or spreading codes describes TDM and CDM respectively.

questions.q: 64 QAM is described as using how many phases and amplitudes?
o: 64 phases and 1 amplitude
8 phases and 8 amplitudes
16 phases and 8 amplitudes
4 phases and 16 amplitudes
questions.e: 64 QAM is described as using 4 phases and 16 amplitudes, while 128 QAM uses 16 phases and 8 amplitudes. Both illustrate how QAM scales by combining phase and amplitude variation.

questions.q: In the QAM levels description, what results from using four-level ASK on each of the two streams?
o: A two-state system
A combined stream in one of 64 states
A combined stream in one of 16 states
A four-state system
questions.e: Two-level ASK on each of two streams yields a four-state system, while four-level ASK on each yields a combined stream in one of 16 states. Systems with 64 and 256 states have also been implemented, improving data rate for a given bandwidth at the cost of increased potential error rate.

questions.q: Digital modulation is defined as the process of transferring a digital baseband signal over what?
o: A synchronous time division multiplexed frame
A parallel bus of higher width
A dedicated fiber optic wavelength
A higher frequency carrier signal such as a radio frequency band
questions.e: Digital modulation transfers a low frequency digital baseband signal, such as a bitstream from a computer, over a higher frequency carrier signal such as a radio frequency band. It resembles analog modulation except that the baseband signal has discrete amplitude levels, only two for a binary signal.

questions.q: The public telephone system is designed to transmit analog signals in which frequency range?
o: 300 Hz to 20 kHz
3 kHz to 34 kHz
30 Hz to 300 Hz
300 Hz to 3400 Hz
questions.e: The public telephone system is designed to transmit analog signals in the 300 Hz to 3400 Hz band. This voice-grade range is why analog data in electrical form can be sent as baseband signals over such lines easily and cheaply.

questions.q: Which three basic types of analog modulation exist, and why exactly three?
o: ASK, FSK and PSK, because digital data has three states
AM, FM and QAM, because QAM combines the other two
AM, FM and PM, because a carrier has three properties: amplitude, frequency and phase
AM, PM and PCM, because sampling adds a third dimension
questions.e: There are three basic analog modulation types — Amplitude Modulation, Frequency Modulation and Phase Modulation — because a carrier signal has exactly three properties that can be varied: amplitude, frequency and phase. ASK, FSK and PSK are the digital counterparts of the same three choices.

questions.q: Frequency Modulation is defined as varying which quantity in accordance with what?
o: The instantaneous frequency of the carrier, in accordance with the instantaneous amplitude of the message signal
The carrier bandwidth, in accordance with the message bandwidth
The instantaneous phase of the carrier, in accordance with the instantaneous phase of the message
The instantaneous amplitude of the carrier, in accordance with the instantaneous frequency of the message
questions.e: Frequency Modulation varies the instantaneous frequency of the carrier signal in accordance with the instantaneous amplitude of the message signal. Amplitude and Phase Modulation follow the same pattern, varying the carrier's amplitude or phase respectively against the message amplitude.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares analog and digital modulation?
o: Analog modulation is more expensive to implement but produces more accurate output
Digital modulation is cheaper and less accurate than analog modulation
Both have exactly two valid values, differing only in cost
Analog modulation has a range of valid values while digital modulation has only two, and analog is cheaper to implement while digital produces more accurate output
questions.e: Analog modulation takes an analog signal with a range of valid values, whereas digital modulation takes a digital signal with only two; analog modulation is cheaper to implement, but digital modulation produces more accurate output. The accuracy-versus-cost split is the key contrast.

questions.q: In analog modulation, what must be true of the baseband signal?
o: It is always analog
It must be a square wave
It is always digital
It may be either, depending on the carrier
questions.e: In analog modulation the baseband signal is always analog, such as an audio or TV signal transferred over a higher frequency carrier. Digital modulation is the counterpart where the baseband signal has discrete amplitude levels.

questions.q: Analog to digital conversion is performed using which device?
o: A hypervisor
A modem
A multiplexer
A codec (coder-decoder)
questions.e: Analog to digital conversion is done using a codec, short for coder-decoder. The two principal codec techniques named are Pulse Code Modulation and Delta Modulation.

questions.q: The sampling theorem underlying PCM states that a signal must be sampled at what rate to retain all its information?
o: At a rate higher than half the highest signal frequency
At a rate higher than twice the highest signal frequency
At a rate equal to the channel bandwidth
At a rate equal to the highest signal frequency
questions.e: The sampling theorem states that if a signal is sampled at regular intervals at a rate higher than twice the highest signal frequency, the samples contain all the information of the original signal. This is why voice data limited to below 4000 Hz needs 8000 samples per second.

questions.q: Voice data is limited to below 4000 Hz. How many samples per second are sufficient to characterise the voice signal?
questions.e: Because the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency, 8000 samples per second suffice for voice limited to below 4000 Hz. These analog samples are called Pulse Amplitude Modulation samples before being assigned binary codes.

questions.q: The analog samples produced before binary coding in PCM are known as what?
o: Pulse Code Modulation samples
Pulse Amplitude Modulation (PAM) samples
Quantized samples
Delta samples
questions.e: The analog samples taken at regular intervals are called Pulse Amplitude Modulation samples. To convert them to digital form, each must then be assigned a binary code, which is the quantizing and coding stage of PCM.

questions.q: In PCM, the original signal cannot be recovered exactly after quantizing. What is this effect called?
o: Intermodulation noise
Delay distortion
Slope overload noise
Quantizing error or quantizing noise
questions.e: Because each sample is quantized into a discrete level, the original signal is only approximated and cannot be exactly recovered; this is quantizing error or quantizing noise. Slope overload noise is a different effect specific to delta modulation.

questions.q: An 8-bit PCM sample gives how many quantization levels?
questions.e: An 8-bit sample gives 256 quantization levels, since 2^8 = 256. More bits per sample reduce quantizing error but increase the required data rate.

questions.q: What is stated as a principal disadvantage of PCM?
o: It has no error detection capability
It cannot represent voice signals
It requires large bandwidth
It transmits only one bit per sample
questions.e: A stated disadvantage of PCM is that it requires large bandwidth. Delta modulation, by contrast, is noted for requiring minimum bandwidth for transmission.

questions.q: In nonlinear encoding, how are quantization levels distributed and why?
