o: More quantizing steps for low amplitude signals and fewer for large amplitude signals, to reduce overall signal distortion
Equally spaced, to simplify the encoder design
More quantizing steps for large amplitude signals, to preserve peaks
Randomly spaced, to spread quantizing noise across frequencies
questions.e: Nonlinear encoding uses a greater number of quantizing steps for low amplitude signals and fewer for large amplitude signals, reducing overall signal distortion. It exists because with equal spacing the mean absolute error per sample is the same regardless of signal level, so lower amplitude values end up relatively more distorted.

questions.q: In Delta Modulation, how is the analog signal approximated and what is transmitted?
o: By a staircase function moving up or down by one quantization level per sampling interval, transmitting one bit per sample
By a Fourier series, transmitting the coefficients
By a piecewise linear interpolation, transmitting two bits per sample
By a sine wave fitted to each interval, transmitting eight bits per sample
questions.e: Delta Modulation approximates the analog signal with a staircase function that moves up or down by one quantization level at each sampling interval, generating 1 if the sampled waveform exceeds the staircase and 0 otherwise, so one bit per sample is transmitted with a fixed step size. Its two important parameters are the step size and the sampling rate.

questions.q: In Delta Modulation, slope overload noise occurs under which condition?
o: When the analog waveform is changing slowly
When the analog waveform is changing more rapidly than the staircase can follow
When the step size is too large
When the sampling rate exceeds the Nyquist rate
questions.e: Slope overload noise occurs when the analog waveform changes more rapidly than the staircase function can follow. Quantizing noise is the complementary problem, arising when the analog waveform changes slowly.

questions.q: What is the trade-off in choosing the step size for Delta Modulation?
o: Quantizing noise increases as step size increases, while slope overload noise increases as step size decreases
Both decrease as step size increases
Both quantizing noise and slope overload noise increase as step size increases
Step size affects only the sampling rate, not noise
questions.e: Quantizing noise increases as the step size increases, while slope overload noise increases as the step size decreases, so the two must be balanced. This opposing relationship is why step size cannot simply be minimised or maximised.

questions.q: Noise power density N0 is given by which formula, and what is Boltzmann's constant?
questions.e: Noise power density is N0 = kT watts per hertz of bandwidth, where k is Boltzmann's constant, 1.38 × 10^-23 J/K, and T is temperature in kelvins. Room temperature is usually specified as 290 K for this calculation.

questions.q: Bandwidth efficiency, also called information density or spectral efficiency, is calculated as which ratio?
o: Bit rate divided by transmission bandwidth
Signal power divided by noise power
Transmission bandwidth divided by bit rate
Bit rate multiplied by transmission bandwidth
questions.e: Bandwidth efficiency is bit rate divided by transmission bandwidth, expressed as R/BT. It is used to measure and compare the performance of one digital modulation technique against another.

questions.q: The ratio Eb/N0 represents which quantity, and what is it used for?
o: Bandwidth divided by data rate, used to size channels
Bit rate to baud rate, used to determine signal levels
Signal power to noise power, used to compute channel capacity
Signal energy per bit to noise power density per hertz, used as the standard quality measure for digital communication system performance
questions.e: Eb/N0 is the ratio of signal energy per bit to noise power density per hertz, and serves as the standard quality measure for digital communication system performance. It relates to signal-to-noise ratio by (Eb/N0)dB = (SNR)dB − (R/BT)dB.

questions.q: In the theoretical bit error rate curves for various encoding schemes, which schemes are plotted as sharing a single curve?
o: NRZ with biphase, and AMI with pseudoternary
NRZ with AMI, and biphase with pseudoternary
All four schemes share one common curve
PSK with AMI, and QPSK with NRZ
questions.e: The theoretical BER curves group NRZ together with biphase on one curve and AMI together with pseudoternary on another, with PSK and QPSK plotted as a further pairing. Schemes sharing a curve have identical theoretical error performance against Eb/N0 despite differing in spectrum and synchronization behaviour.

questions.q: Which summary statement correctly pairs a data-and-signal combination with its basic techniques?
o: Digital data to analog signal: PCM and Delta Modulation
Analog data to digital signals: ASK, FSK and PSK
Analog data to analog signals: AM, FM and PM
Digital data to digital signal: AM, FM and PM
questions.e: Analog data modulated onto a carrier to produce an analog signal in a different frequency band uses AM, FM and PM. Digital data to analog signal uses ASK, FSK and PSK via a modem, while analog data to digital signal uses PCM and Delta Modulation.

questions.q: For a receiver to sample incoming bits properly, what must it know?
o: The encryption key used by the sender
The routing path taken by the data
The topology of the sending network
The arrival time and duration of each bit it receives
questions.e: The receiver must know the arrival time and duration of each bit in order to sample them properly, which means it must know the rate at which bits are being received. Mismatch between the transmitter's and receiver's clocks is precisely what causes sampling to fail.

questions.q: If data is transmitted at 1 Mbps, how often is one bit transmitted as measured by the sender's clock?
o: Every 1 microsecond
Every 1 millisecond
Every 1 nanosecond
Every 10 microseconds
questions.e: At one million bits per second, one bit is transmitted every 1/10^6 second, that is every 1 microsecond, so sampling would occur once per microsecond. A problem arises if the receiver times its samples on its own clock and the two clocks are not precisely aligned.

questions.q: In asynchronous transmission, how is each character handled?
o: Each character carries its own CRC
Characters are grouped into frames with a shared preamble
Each character is treated independently and begins with a start bit that alerts the receiver
Characters are transmitted continuously with no delimiters
questions.e: In asynchronous transmission each character of data is treated independently and begins with a start bit alerting the receiver that a character is arriving; the receiver samples each bit then looks for the next character's start. This is why it does not work well for long blocks, where the receiver's clock could drift out of synchronization.

questions.q: In the asynchronous transmission of the ASCII letter 'A', what is the framing structure described?
o: Start bit 0, data bits 01000010, stop bit 1
Start bit 1, data bits 01000001, stop bit 0
Start bit 1, data bits 01000010, stop bit 0
Start bit 0, data bits 01000001, stop bit 1
questions.e: The example uses a start bit of 0, the data bits 01000001 representing 'A' in ASCII, and a stop bit of 1. The start bit prepares the receiver to accept data and the stop bit signals the end of the character, giving the receiver a moment before the next one.

questions.q: Asynchronous transmission is described as suitable for which kind of traffic?
o: Continuous high-rate streaming
Data with large gaps, such as from a keyboard
Bulk file transfer over long distances
Synchronous optical backbone links
questions.e: Asynchronous transmission suits data with large gaps, such as keyboard input, and is used in serial communication including UART and asynchronous serial ports. It is flexible and does not require precise synchronization, which is its main appeal.

questions.q: In synchronous transmission, how are the start and end of a block indicated?
o: By parity bits at both ends
By a preamble and a postamble
By a change in signal polarity
By start and stop bits on each character
questions.e: Synchronous transmission sends a block of data as a frame and uses a preamble and postamble to indicate the start and end of the block. Clocks must also be synchronized, either using a separate clock line or by embedding the clock signal in the data.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares synchronous and asynchronous transmission?
o: Synchronous is fast and costly with no gaps between data; asynchronous is slow and economical with gaps between data
Synchronous is slow and economical; asynchronous is fast and costly
Asynchronous makes more efficient use of the transmission line
Both leave the transmission line empty during gaps
questions.e: Synchronous transmission is fast, costly and leaves no gap between data, making efficient use of the transmission line; asynchronous is slow and economical, with gaps between data during which the line remains empty. Efficiency and cost pull in opposite directions between the two schemes.

questions.q: Which factor is cited as making synchronous communication more expensive to implement?
o: It cannot use error detection codes
It requires a separate physical line per character
It requires more transmission media per link
It relies on accurate timing and synchronized clocks, demanding specialized and more expensive hardware
questions.e: Synchronous communication depends heavily on accurate timing and synchronized clocks, which requires specialized and more expensive hardware, plus more sophisticated circuitry and protocols. Building and maintaining infrastructure such as SONET or SDH adds further cost, and its lower tolerance of errors demands extra detection and correction.

questions.q: HDLC contains 48 bits of control, preamble and postamble. For a 1000-character block of data, what is the percentage overhead?
o: About 6%
About 0.06%
About 4.8%
About 0.6%
questions.e: With 48 overhead bits and 1000 × 8 = 8000 data bits, the overhead is 48/8048 × 100% ≈ 0.6%. The overhead becomes proportionally smaller as the block grows, which is why synchronous framing is efficient for large blocks.

questions.q: In the two types of transmission error, what distinguishes a burst error from a single bit error?
o: A burst error changes multiple bits of a binary value and is common and more difficult to deal with
A burst error changes one bit; a single bit error changes several
A burst error is always detected by a single parity bit
A burst error occurs only in analog transmission
questions.e: A single bit error means one bit value is changed, whereas a burst error means multiple bits of a binary value are changed; burst errors are common and more difficult to deal with. This difficulty is why stronger codes such as CRC are preferred over simple parity.

questions.q: If k is the number of bits in the data block and n is the number of bits transmitted, what does (n − k) represent, and what general rule applies?
o: The number of data bits, with the rule (n − k) > k
The parity of the block, with no general rule
The number of bits used for error detection, with the rule (n − k) < k
The number of frames transmitted, with the rule (n − k) = k
questions.e: The quantity (n − k) is the number of bits added for error detection, and the general rule is that (n − k) < k, so the check bits remain a minority of the transmission. The three common detection techniques named are VRC or parity check, LRC, and CRC.

questions.q: Vertical Redundancy Check is another name for which technique?
o: Checksum
Cyclic redundancy check
Hamming code
Parity check
questions.e: Vertical Redundancy Check is another name for the parity check, in which a parity bit is added to each character. It comes in even and odd flavours depending on whether the total count of ones including the parity bit is made even or odd.

questions.q: Using even parity, the data 10101 is transmitted as which of the following?
questions.e: The data 10101 contains three ones, an odd count, so an even parity scheme appends a 1 to make the total count four, giving 101011. Under odd parity the same data would instead be transmitted as 101010.

questions.q: Using odd parity, the data 10100 is transmitted as which of the following?
questions.e: The data 10100 contains two ones, an even count, so odd parity appends a 1 to make the total three, giving 101001. Under even parity the same data would be transmitted as 101000.

questions.q: In Longitudinal Redundancy Check, how are the parity bits computed?
o: One parity bit per character, appended to each character
The block is arranged as a list of rows and a parity bit is calculated for every column
A single parity bit is computed over the entire block
Parity is computed diagonally across the block
questions.e: In LRC the block of data is organized as a list of rows and a parity bit is calculated for every column, producing a set of parity bits for the whole block that is transmitted along with the data. VRC differs by attaching one check bit to each individual character.

questions.q: When is VRC preferable to LRC, according to the granularity of error detection?
o: VRC for analog data; LRC for digital data
VRC when checking a block as a whole; LRC when checking each character separately
VRC when checking each character separately; LRC when checking a block of multiple characters using a single check character
VRC for burst errors; LRC for single bit errors
questions.e: VRC is used when you want to check each character separately, since each character carries its own parity bit, while LRC is used to check a block of multiple characters by creating a single check character from a combination of their bits. Both detect errors during transmission but differ in the level of granularity.

questions.q: Cyclic Redundancy Check is based on which arithmetic operation?
o: Modulo 2 binary division using XOR rather than subtraction
Bitwise AND of the data with the generator
Two's complement addition
Ordinary decimal long division
questions.e: CRC is based on binary division, specifically modulo 2 division which uses XOR instead of subtraction. It is described as the most common and most powerful error detecting code.

questions.q: In CRC, the sequence of (n − k) bits generated by the transmitter is called what?
o: The parity block
The preamble
The Frame Check Sequence (FCS)
The codeword
questions.e: The transmitter generates an (n − k) bit sequence called the Frame Check Sequence. For a data block of k bits, n bits in total are transmitted, the extra bits being this FCS.

questions.q: A CRC generator is expressed as an algebraic polynomial. What rule converts it into a bit pattern?
o: The polynomial degree alone determines the pattern
The coefficient gives the bit position and the power gives the bit value
Each term contributes two bits, one for power and one for coefficient
The power of each term gives the position of the bit and the coefficient gives the value of the bit
questions.e: The rule is that the power of each term gives the position of the bit and the coefficient gives the value of the bit. Applying it to x^7 + x^6 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1 yields the binary pattern 11011011.

questions.q: Which polynomial corresponds to the widely used CRC-CCITT standard?
questions.e: CRC-CCITT is X^16 + X^12 + X^5 + 1. CRC-16 is the different 16-degree polynomial X^16 + X^15 + X^2 + 1, so the two must not be confused despite sharing a degree.

questions.q: At the sender side, how many zeros are appended to the data unit before the CRC division is performed?
o: A number equal to the number of bits in the CRC generator
A number equal to the number of data bits
Always eight zeros
A number one less than the number of bits in the CRC generator
questions.e: A string of n zeros is appended, where n is one less than the number of bits in the CRC generator. After division, the remainder obtained is the CRC, which then replaces those appended zeros.

questions.q: A bit stream 1101011011 is transmitted using standard CRC with generator polynomial x^4 + x + 1. What is the generator's binary encoding and how many zeros are appended?
o: 11011, with four zeros appended
1011, with three zeros appended
10011, with five zeros appended
10011, with four zeros appended
questions.e: The polynomial x^4 + x + 1 encodes as 10011, which is five bits long, so four zeros are appended, giving 11010110110000. The count of appended zeros is always one fewer than the generator's bit length.

questions.q: For the bit stream 1101011011 with generator x^4 + x + 1, the CRC remainder is 1110. What is the actual bit string transmitted?
questions.e: The transmitted codeword replaces the four appended zeros of 11010110110000 with the CRC remainder 1110, giving 11010110111110. The codeword is not lengthened further, since the zeros were placeholders for the CRC.

questions.q: A bit stream 10011101 is sent with generator polynomial x^3 + 1, whose binary encoding is 1001 and which yields CRC 100. What codeword is transmitted?
questions.e: Three zeros are appended to give 10011101000, and the CRC 100 replaces those zeros, producing 10011101100. The generator 1001 is four bits, so exactly three zeros are appended.

questions.q: Continuing that example, the third bit from the left is inverted in transit so the receiver gets 10111101100. How does the receiver detect the error?
o: By recomputing the parity of each character
By checking that the frame length is unchanged
By comparing the received data against a stored copy
By dividing the received codeword by the same generator polynomial and finding a non-zero remainder
questions.e: The receiver divides the received codeword by the same generator polynomial; a non-zero remainder indicates an error, so the data is rejected and retransmission requested. A remainder of zero would instead lead the receiver to assume no error occurred and accept the data.

questions.q: Why is error correction sometimes preferred over error detection alone?
o: Because detection codes cannot find burst errors
Because detection cannot be implemented in hardware
Because detection requires retransmission, which is especially expensive on wireless links with high error rates
Because correction requires fewer check bits than detection
questions.e: Error detection alone requires retransmission of the data, and retransmission is especially expensive on wireless links, which have high error rates and therefore generate many retransmissions. Bandwidth being expensive is the underlying motivation for correcting errors in place where possible.

questions.q: What distinguishes backward error correction from forward error correction?
o: Backward correction uses an error-correcting code at the receiver; forward correction requests retransmission
Both correct errors locally, differing only in code strength
Backward correction requests retransmission of the data unit; forward correction uses an error-correcting code that automatically corrects errors at the receiver
Both request retransmission, differing only in timing
questions.e: In backward error correction, once an error is discovered the receiver asks the sender to retransmit the entire data unit; in forward error correction, the receiver uses an error-correcting code that automatically corrects the errors. Forward correction avoids the round trip entirely, which is why it suits high-latency or high-error links.

questions.q: The Hamming distance between two n-bit binary sequences is defined as what?
o: The number of bits set to 1 in either sequence
The number of bit positions in which the two sequences disagree
The number of leading bits the two sequences share
The arithmetic difference between the two values
questions.e: The Hamming distance between two n-bit sequences is the number of bit positions in which they disagree. For example, V1 = 10011011 and V2 = 11000101 differ in five positions, so d(V1, V2) = 5.

questions.q: Given the codebook 00→00000, 01→00111, 10→11001, 11→11110, a receiver gets 00100. Which codeword was most likely transmitted?
questions.e: The received word 00100 differs from 00000 in one position, from 00111 in two, from 11001 in four, and from 11110 in three, so 00000 is the closest valid codeword and is selected. The decoding rule is to choose the valid codeword at minimum Hamming distance from what was received.

questions.q: In an (n, k) block code, how many of the possible codewords are valid?
o: 2^n out of 2^k possible
2^k out of 2^n possible
n out of k possible
All 2^n are valid
questions.e: An (n, k) block code encodes k data bits into an n-bit codeword, so out of 2^n possible bit patterns only 2^k are valid codewords. The redundancy of the unused patterns is what makes detection and correction possible.

questions.q: In the CRC check at the receiver, what does a remainder of zero signify?
o: That no error occurred during transmission, so the data is accepted
That an error occurred and retransmission is needed
That the frame was truncated
That the generator polynomial was wrong
questions.e: A remainder of zero leads the receiver to assume no error occurred during transmission and to accept the data. A non-zero remainder means an error is assumed, the data is rejected, and the sender is asked to retransmit.

questions.q: What is the purpose of flow control at the data link layer?
o: To assign addresses to stations on a link
To convert digital data into analog signals
To ensure the sending entity does not overwhelm the receiving entity
To select the best path for each frame
questions.e: Flow control ensures the sending entity does not overwhelm the receiving entity. Flow control, error detection and error control together are handled by a control layer known as the data link control protocol, the most common of which is HDLC.

questions.q: What distinguishes transmission time from propagation time?
o: Transmission time applies to analog links and propagation time to digital links
Transmission time is the time taken to emit all bits of a frame onto the medium; propagation time is the time for a bit to travel from source to destination
Transmission time is the time for a bit to travel from source to destination; propagation time is the time to emit all bits of a frame
Both refer to the same quantity measured at different layers
questions.e: Transmission time is the time taken to emit all the bits of a frame onto the medium, while propagation time is the time for a single bit to travel from source to destination. Link utilization analysis compares the two, normalising transmission time to 1 and calling propagation time a.

questions.q: In stop-and-wait flow control, how can the destination halt the flow of data?
o: By reducing its window size to zero
By sending a reject frame
By closing the physical connection
By simply not sending an acknowledgement
questions.e: In stop-and-wait, the source waits for an acknowledgement before sending the next frame, so the destination can stop the flow simply by not sending an ACK. The mechanism is the simplest form of flow control precisely because it needs no additional signalling.

questions.q: Why is stop-and-wait flow control described as inefficient?
o: Because each frame sent and acknowledged uses the entire time needed to traverse the link, so distant devices waste much time waiting for ACKs
Because it requires a separate clock line
Because it cannot detect errors
Because it requires more check bits than sliding window
questions.e: Each frame sent and each acknowledgement returned consumes the full link traversal time, so when two devices are far apart a great deal of time is wasted waiting for ACKs, increasing total transmission time. This inefficiency is particularly bad at high data rates or over long distances.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as a reason for splitting a large block of data into smaller frames?
o: Because of limited buffer size at the receiver, and so that errors are detected sooner with only smaller frames needing retransmission
To allow the use of analog transmission
To eliminate the need for acknowledgements
To increase the propagation time of each bit
questions.e: Fragmentation into smaller frames is motivated by limited receiver buffer size, earlier error detection since a whole frame must be received before checking, smaller retransmissions on error, and preventing one station from occupying a shared medium for long periods. It does not remove the need for acknowledgements.

questions.q: In sliding window flow control, what does the acknowledgement indicate?
o: The number of the last frame successfully received
The number of the next frame expected
The identity of the frame in error
The total number of frames still buffered
questions.e: The acknowledgement, denoted RR for Receive Ready, includes the number of the next frame expected. This convention lets a single acknowledgement confirm every frame up to that point at once.

questions.q: With a 3-bit sequence number field, what is the maximum sliding window size?
o: Four frames
Seven frames
Eight frames
Three frames
questions.e: A 3-bit sequence number field permits a maximum window size of seven frames. Although three bits can express eight distinct numbers, the window is limited to one fewer so that acknowledgements remain unambiguous.

questions.q: In the sliding window example, station A has transmitted frames F0, F1 and F2 without acknowledgement. What happens to its window?
o: It shrinks to four frames, beginning with frame number 3, while A keeps copies of the three transmitted frames
It resets to begin again at frame 0
It closes completely until an acknowledgement arrives
It expands to ten frames to compensate
questions.e: After transmitting three frames without acknowledgement, A's window shrinks from seven to four frames beginning at frame number 3, and A retains copies of the three transmitted frames in case retransmission is needed. When B then sends RR 3, A's window reopens to seven frames still beginning at frame 3 and the buffered copies may be discarded.

questions.q: In the sliding window example, what does an acknowledgement of RR 3 from station B mean?
o: Only frame 3 has been received so far
B can accept exactly three more frames
Frame 3 was received in error and must be resent
All frames up through frame number 2 were received and B is ready to receive frame number 3
questions.e: RR 3 means B has received all frames up through frame number 2 and is ready to receive frame number 3, and in fact is prepared to receive seven frames beginning with frame 3. The number in an RR always names the next frame expected, not the last one received.

questions.q: Error control distinguishes which two types of error?
o: Lost frames that fail to arrive, and damaged frames in which some bits are in error
Single bit errors and burst errors
Detected errors and undetected errors
Syntax errors and semantic errors
questions.e: At the level of error control, the two types are lost frames, which fail to arrive at all, and damaged frames, in which some bits are in error. Single bit and burst errors are a separate classification describing the bit-level pattern of corruption.

questions.q: Which set of mechanisms are collectively referred to as Automatic Repeat Request?
o: Encapsulation, segmentation, reassembly and multiplexing
Framing, bit stuffing and flag detection
Parity checking, checksums and hashing
Error detection, positive acknowledgement, retransmission after timeout, and negative acknowledgement with retransmission
questions.e: ARQ collectively names error detection such as CRC, positive acknowledgement from the receiver on success, retransmission after timeout when a timer expires, and negative acknowledgement with retransmission. A NACK lets the receiver signal an error immediately rather than making the sender wait for a timeout.

questions.q: Which three versions of ARQ have been standardized?
o: Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N and Selective-Reject
Positive, Negative and Cumulative
Stop-and-Wait, Sliding Window and Flooding
Static, Dynamic and Adaptive
questions.e: The three standardized ARQ versions are Stop-and-Wait ARQ, Go-Back-N ARQ and Selective-Reject ARQ. Each extends either the stop-and-wait or the sliding-window flow control scheme.

questions.q: In Stop-and-Wait ARQ, why are frames alternately numbered 0 and 1?
o: To allow two frames to be outstanding at once
To indicate the priority of each frame
So the receiver can recognise and discard a duplicate that arises when an acknowledgement is damaged
To identify which of two channels carries the frame
questions.e: If an acknowledgement is damaged the sender does not recognise it and retransmits, so the receiver would get two copies; alternate numbering with 0 and 1, matched by alternating ACK0 and ACK1, lets the receiver recognise the duplicate and discard it. The scheme's advantage is simplicity, its drawback poor bandwidth utilization since only one frame is outstanding at a time.

questions.q: In Go-Back-N ARQ, what does the destination do after detecting an error in a frame?
o: Replies with a rejection for the frame and discards that frame and all future frames until the error frame is received correctly
Terminates the connection and restarts
Corrects the frame using an error-correcting code
Buffers all subsequent frames and requests only the damaged one
questions.e: On detecting an error, the destination replies with REJ for that frame and discards it along with all subsequent frames until the errored frame is correctly received, so the source must go back and retransmit that frame and all frames after it. Go-Back-N also handles damaged or lost data frames, RRs and REJs.

questions.q: What is the principal advantage of Selective-Reject ARQ, and what is the cost?
o: It works without buffering, but increases latency
It eliminates the need for acknowledgements, but requires more bandwidth
It removes the need for sequence numbers, but reduces reliability
It minimizes the amount of retransmission, but both receiver and sender become more complex
questions.e: Selective-Reject retransmits only the specifically rejected frames via SREJ, so it minimizes retransmission, but the receiver must buffer post-SREJ frames and reorder them, and the sender needs extra logic to send a frame out of sequence. Both endpoints therefore become more complex than in Go-Back-N.

questions.q: Which ARQ scheme is based on sliding-window flow control and uses REJ to signal an error?
o: Flooding ARQ
Stop-and-Wait ARQ
Go-Back-N ARQ
Selective-Reject ARQ
questions.e: Go-Back-N ARQ is based on sliding-window flow control and signals errors with REJ, meaning reject. Selective-Reject also builds on sliding window but uses SREJ to reject frames individually.

questions.q: HDLC originated from which protocol, developed by which company?
o: Frame Relay, developed by Cisco
SDLC, developed by IBM
LAPB, developed by AT&T
LLC, developed by Xerox
questions.e: HDLC derives from Synchronous Data Link Control (SDLC), developed by IBM and later standardized by ISO as High Level Data Link Control. It is described as the most important and most widely used data-link control protocol, with many other protocols based on it.

questions.q: Which of the three HDLC station types acts either as a primary or a secondary depending on the nature and direction of transmission?
o: Secondary station
Combined station
Peer station
Primary station
questions.e: A combined station acts as either primary or secondary depending on the nature and direction of transmission, and sends both commands and responses. A primary station has complete control of the link and sends commands, while a secondary is under its control and issues responses.

questions.q: What distinguishes an unbalanced from a balanced HDLC link configuration?
o: Unbalanced supports only half duplex; balanced supports only full duplex
Unbalanced uses bit stuffing; balanced does not
Unbalanced has two combined stations; balanced has one primary and several secondaries
Unbalanced has one primary and one or more secondary stations; balanced has two combined stations
questions.e: An unbalanced configuration has one primary and one or more secondary stations, while a balanced configuration has two combined stations. Both configurations support full duplex and half duplex operation.

questions.q: In which HDLC transfer mode may a secondary station initiate transmission without permission from the primary, while the configuration remains unbalanced?
o: Synchronous Balanced Mode (SBM)
Normal Response Mode (NRM)
Asynchronous Balanced Mode (ABM)
Asynchronous Response Mode (ARM)
questions.e: Asynchronous Response Mode keeps the unbalanced configuration but allows a secondary to initiate transmission without permission from the primary. In Normal Response Mode, by contrast, the primary sends commands and a secondary can only respond.

questions.q: Which HDLC transfer mode is described as the most widely used, and why?
o: Normal Response Mode, because it is simplest
Asynchronous Response Mode, because secondaries have freedom
Asynchronous Balanced Mode, because either station may initiate transmission and it makes more efficient use of full-duplex
Normal Response Mode, because it supports the most secondaries
questions.e: Asynchronous Balanced Mode uses a balanced configuration in which either station may initiate transmission without receiving permission, making more efficient use of full-duplex operation, and it is the most widely used mode. NRM and ARM both retain the unbalanced primary-secondary relationship.

questions.q: What is the HDLC flag pattern used to delimit frames at both ends?
questions.e: The HDLC flag is 01111110, used to delimit the frame at both ends and possibly to close one frame while opening another. The receiver hunts for this sequence to synchronize, and bit stuffing prevents the same pattern appearing accidentally in the data.

questions.q: How does HDLC bit stuffing prevent the flag pattern from appearing in the data?
o: A zero is stuffed after five consecutive ones
The data is inverted whenever a flag is detected
The flag is transmitted twice to distinguish it
A one is inserted after every four consecutive zeros
questions.e: When five consecutive ones occur in the data, a zero is stuffed after them, so the six-consecutive-ones pattern of the flag can never arise accidentally. The receiver removes the stuffed zeros to recover the original data.

questions.q: In the HDLC address field, what does an address of all ones (11111111) signify?
o: A request for connection establishment
A broadcast address allowing the primary to send a frame for reception by all secondaries
An invalid or reserved address
The address of the primary station itself
questions.e: An all-ones address is interpreted as an all-stations address in both basic and extended formats, allowing the primary to broadcast a frame for reception by all secondaries. The field is usually 8 bits and may be extended in multiples of 7 bits, with the least significant bit of each octet indicating whether it is the last octet.

questions.q: In the extended HDLC address format, what does the least significant bit of each octet indicate?
o: Whether the address belongs to a primary or secondary station
The parity of the address field
Whether that octet is or is not the last octet of the address field
Whether the frame is a command or a response
questions.e: The least significant bit of each octet is 1 or 0 to indicate whether it is or is not the last octet of the address field. This allows addresses to be extended in multiples of 7 usable bits.

questions.q: HDLC defines three frame types distinguished by their control field. Which bits identify each?
o: I-frame: first two bits 00; S-frame: first two bits 01; U-frame: first two bits 10
I-frame: first bit 0; S-frame: first two bits 10; U-frame: first two bits 11
I-frame: first bit 1; S-frame: first bit 0; U-frame: first two bits 11
I-frame: first bit 1; S-frame: first two bits 01; U-frame: first two bits 00
questions.e: An I-frame (Information) has a first bit of 0 and carries information, an S-frame (Supervisory) begins 10 and plays a role in error and flow control, and a U-frame (Unnumbered) begins 11 and handles miscellaneous activities such as link management. The frame type is therefore determined entirely by the control field's leading bits.

questions.q: In the 8-bit HDLC control field, what do N(S) and N(R) denote?
o: Number of stations and number of retransmissions
Send sequence number and receive sequence number
Network source and network receiver identifiers
Negative and positive acknowledgement flags
questions.e: N(S) is the send sequence number and N(R) is the receive sequence number. The control field also carries the Poll/Final bit, and S bits for supervisory functions or M bits for unnumbered functions depending on the frame type.

questions.q: Which HDLC fields carry the information field, and what error detection does the FCS use?
o: Only U-frames; a Hamming code
Only S-frames; an 8-bit checksum
Only I-frames and some U-frames; a 16-bit CRC with an optional 32-bit CRC
All three frame types; a simple parity bit
questions.e: The information field is present only in I-frames and some U-frames and is of variable length up to a system-defined maximum, while the Frame Check Sequence uses a 16-bit cyclic redundancy check with an optional 32-bit CRC. The FCS provides error detection rather than correction.

questions.q: What are the three phases of HDLC operation?
o: Initialization, data transfer with flow and error control, and disconnect
Synchronize, transmit and verify
Request, acknowledge and confirm
Establish, maintain and terminate
questions.e: HDLC operation consists of initialization, data transfer with control flow and error control, and disconnect. Data transfer begins with I-frames numbered from sequence number 0, with S-frames used for flow and error control.

questions.q: During HDLC initialization, what does the other side send if it accepts the request, and what if it rejects?
o: Unnumbered Acknowledgement (UA) if accepted; Disconnected Mode (DM) if rejected
SREJ if accepted; DISC if rejected
ACK0 if accepted; ACK1 if rejected
RR if accepted; REJ if rejected
questions.e: If the request is accepted the HDLC module transmits an Unnumbered Acknowledgement frame back to the initiating side; if rejected, a Disconnected Mode frame is sent. The initialization command also specifies which of the three modes — NRM, ABM or ARM — is being requested.

questions.q: How is an HDLC connection disconnected?
o: By issuing a DISC frame, which the other side must accept by replying with an unnumbered acknowledgement
By ceasing to send frames until a timeout expires
By reducing the window size to zero
By sending an all-ones address frame
questions.e: HDLC disconnects by issuing a DISC frame, and the other side must accept it by replying with an unnumbered acknowledgement (UA). A disconnect may be commanded deliberately or arise from some fault.

questions.q: How does Logical Link Control differ from HDLC in its station relationships and error detection?
o: LLC has combined stations only and performs no error detection
LLC is identical to HDLC apart from frame size
LLC has no primary and secondary since all stations are peers, and error detection occurs at the MAC sublayer
LLC has a strict primary-secondary hierarchy and detects errors at the network layer
questions.e: In LLC there is no primary and secondary because all stations are peers, and error detection is performed at the MAC sublayer, whereas HDLC defines primary, secondary and combined stations. LLC also uses a different frame format and acts as the interface between the network layer and the MAC sublayer.

questions.q: What is the difference between a multiplexer and a demultiplexer?
o: A multiplexer combines multiple signals into one signal; a demultiplexer separates the multiplexed signals
A multiplexer separates combined signals; a demultiplexer combines them
A multiplexer works on analog signals only; a demultiplexer on digital only
Both combine signals, differing only in direction of travel
questions.e: A multiplexer is a device that combines multiple signals into one signal, and a demultiplexer separates the multiplexed signals again. They occupy opposite ends of a shared transmission link.

questions.q: In the classification of multiplexing techniques, which two fall under the analog branch?
o: Frequency Division Multiplexing and Time Division Multiplexing
Frequency Division Multiplexing and Wavelength Division Multiplexing
Time Division Multiplexing and Code Division Multiplexing
Synchronous TDM and Asynchronous TDM
questions.e: Frequency Division Multiplexing and Wavelength Division Multiplexing are the analog techniques, while Time Division Multiplexing is the digital branch, which further divides into Synchronous and Asynchronous TDM. FDM and WDM differ in that FDM assigns frequency bands while WDM assigns wavelengths of light.

questions.q: In Frequency Division Multiplexing, what is done to each input signal?
o: Each is modulated with a carrier frequency to change its frequency characteristics
Each is assigned a unique mathematical code
Each is assigned a time slot in rotation
Each is converted to a different wavelength of light
questions.e: FDM is an analog technique in which every input signal is modulated with a carrier frequency to change its frequency, so the signals occupy distinct bands. Assigning time slots is TDM, and assigning codes is Code Division Multiplexing.

questions.q: Which application of FDM allows multiple television channels to be delivered over a single coaxial cable?
o: Broadcasting over the airwaves
Wireless cellular communication
Cable Television (CATV)
Optical backbone transmission
questions.e: Cable television uses FDM to deliver multiple channels over the same coaxial cable, assigning each channel a different frequency band. Radio and TV broadcasting and cellular wireless are the other named FDM applications, using the airwaves rather than a shared cable.

questions.q: How does Wavelength Division Multiplexing differ from Frequency Division Multiplexing?
o: WDM uses different wavelengths of light over a single optical fiber, rather than different frequencies
WDM works only over copper cable
WDM is a digital technique while FDM is analog
WDM assigns time slots while FDM assigns frequency bands
questions.e: WDM is an analog technique that combines multiple wavelengths of optical signal to transmit over a single optical fiber, using wavelengths of light instead of the frequency bands FDM uses. Both remain analog multiplexing techniques.

questions.q: WDM is described as crucial to which infrastructure?
o: Long-haul fiber optic networks and the Internet backbone
Satellite broadcast systems
Cable television distribution networks
Cellular radio access networks
questions.e: WDM is used in long-haul fiber optic networks and is crucial to the Internet backbone, enabling high-speed data transmission between cities and countries by multiplexing multiple data streams onto a single fiber. It substantially increases the capacity and efficiency of such networks.

questions.q: What is the defining difference between Synchronous and Asynchronous TDM?
o: Synchronous TDM reassigns empty slots; Asynchronous TDM leaves them empty
Synchronous TDM uses codes; Asynchronous TDM uses frequencies
Synchronous TDM is analog; Asynchronous TDM is digital
Synchronous TDM allows empty time slots and does not reassign them; Asynchronous TDM leaves no slot empty and reassigns them to available signals
questions.e: In Synchronous TDM time slots can be empty and are not reassigned to other available signals, whereas in Asynchronous TDM no slot is left empty because slots are assigned to whichever signals have data. Asynchronous TDM therefore uses the link more efficiently when sources are idle.

questions.q: Code Division Multiplexing is distinguished from the other techniques by which property?
o: It uses wavelengths of light to separate channels
It is a mathematical technique that does not use the physical properties of the signal, assigning every signal a unique identifying code
It uses the frequency of the signal to separate channels
It divides transmission into fixed time slots
questions.e: Code Division Multiplexing is a mathematical technique that does not rely on physical signal properties such as frequency, time or wavelength; instead every signal is assigned a unique code to identify it. Consequently it has no limitation of time or frequency, though it is a complex technique.

questions.q: Which three physical properties of a signal are used by the non-code multiplexing techniques?
o: Frequency, time and wavelength
Bandwidth, latency and jitter
Amplitude, phase and polarity
Voltage, current and power
questions.e: Frequency, time and wavelength are the physical signal properties exploited by FDM, TDM and WDM respectively. Code Division Multiplexing is contrasted against these because it uses none of them, relying on unique codes instead.

questions.q: Time Division Multiplexing is classified as which kind of technique, and how does it allocate the medium?
o: A digital technique in which every transmitter is assigned a time slot to transmit its signal
An analog technique that assigns frequency bands
A mathematical technique that assigns codes
An optical technique that assigns wavelengths
questions.e: TDM is a digital multiplexing technique in which every transmitter is assigned a time slot in which to transmit its signal. FDM and WDM are the analog techniques, dividing by frequency and wavelength respectively.

questions.q: What distinguishes a network from an internetwork?
o: A network spans multiple buildings; an internetwork is confined to one
A network operates at layer 3; an internetwork at layer 2
A network uses cables; an internetwork uses wireless
A network is a group of locally connected computers, whereas an internetwork is a collection of individual networks joined by intermediate devices that functions as a single large network
questions.e: A network is a group of locally connected computers, such as those in an office building, while an internetwork is a collection of individual networks connected by intermediate networking devices so that it functions as one large network. Repeaters, bridges, routers and gateways are the connecting devices involved.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the purposes of having connecting devices?
o: To convert analog data into digital form
To increase the clock speed of attached computers
To encrypt traffic passing between segments
To localize traffic on the network and isolate network problems so they can be diagnosed more easily
questions.e: Connecting devices allow more nodes to be attached, extend the distance a network can span, localize traffic, merge existing networks, and isolate problems for easier diagnosis. Encryption and analog-to-digital conversion are not among their stated purposes.

questions.q: A repeater, also called a regenerator, operates at which OSI layer and performs what function?
o: Network layer; it selects the best path
Physical layer; it regenerates the signal without changing the data in any way
Data link layer; it filters frames by MAC address
Transport layer; it reorders segments
questions.e: A repeater works at the physical layer, taking a stream of bits in the form of a weakened and corrupted signal and creating a fresh signal, without changing the data in any way. It performs no intelligent function such as filtering or path selection.

questions.q: A hub is best described as which of the following?
o: A multiport bridge implemented in hardware
A layer 3 device that forwards packets between networks
A device that translates between incompatible protocols
A multiport repeater, commonly serving as the center of a star topology network
questions.e: A hub is a multiport repeater, and the term hub is generally used instead of repeater when the device serves as the center of a star topology network. A multiport bridge implemented in hardware is a layer 2 switch, a different device.

questions.q: What is the principal disadvantage of a repeater?
o: It introduces excessive latency
It can only connect two devices
It requires manual configuration of routing tables
It cannot filter network traffic, so data arriving at one port is sent out on all other ports regardless of whether it needs to go there
questions.e: A repeater cannot filter network traffic, so bits arriving at one port are sent out on all other ports and passed to all LAN segments whether or not they need to go there. This is what leads to excessive traffic and collisions when segments are joined only by non-filtering devices.

questions.q: What occurs when more than one node attempts to transmit at the same time on a network connected only by non-filtering devices?
o: The repeater buffers one frame until the other completes
The frames are automatically queued and sent in order
A collision occurs, and the data from each device impacts and is damaged
The slower device is disconnected
questions.e: If more than one node transmits simultaneously a collision occurs and the data from each device impacts and is damaged. Bridges address this by dividing the network into segments, which eliminates unnecessary traffic and reduces the chance of collisions.

questions.q: A bridge is described as a computer possessing which hardware?
o: No processor, being purely a passive signal amplifier
A single NIC and a routing table in ROM
Three or more NICs and a dedicated switching fabric
Its own processor, memory and two NICs
questions.e: A bridge is a computer with its own processor, memory and two network interface cards, used to connect two segments of a network. It operates at the physical and data link layers, making it more intelligent than a repeater.

questions.q: If a host on segment 1 wants to communicate with a host on segment 3, what does a bridge do?
o: Blocks the traffic since it crosses a segment boundary
Forwards the frames from segment 1 to segment 3 only, and not to segments 2 and 4
Converts the frames into packets before forwarding them
Forwards the frames to all four segments to guarantee delivery
questions.e: A bridge forwards frames only to the segment concerned, so traffic from segment 1 destined for segment 3 goes there alone and not to segments 2 and 4. This selective forwarding is what minimizes unwanted traffic compared with a repeater.

questions.q: What information does a bridge maintain in its table?
o: Frame sequence numbers mapped to timestamps
IP addresses mapped to next-hop routers
Host addresses mapped to segment numbers
Port numbers mapped to applications
questions.e: A bridge maintains a table mapping host addresses to segment numbers, which it uses to decide on which segment to forward each frame. Because it knows physical addresses of hosts, it can also provide security features and access control.

questions.q: A learning bridge, also called an adaptive bridge, behaves how when it has no table entry for a host?
o: It floods the frame continuously until an acknowledgement arrives
It discards the frame and waits for the administrator to add an entry
It sends the frame to all segments and makes an entry for the source, then records the destination when the response is received
It forwards the frame to the default gateway
questions.e: When there is no entry for a host, a learning bridge sends the frame to all segments and makes an entry for the source address, then adds the destination entry when the response comes back. This contrasts with a simple bridge, whose table must be updated manually whenever a host is added or removed.

questions.q: In the classification of bridges, what is a multiport bridge?
o: A bridge operating at the network layer
A bridge that requires manual table configuration only
A bridge that connects exactly two segments
A simple or learning bridge connecting more than two segments, implemented in hardware as a layer 2 switch
questions.e: A multiport bridge is a simple or learning bridge that connects more than two segments, and implemented in hardware it is a layer 2 switch. A simple bridge by contrast connects just two segments and needs manual table updates.

questions.q: What problem can a bridge itself create when traffic between network segments becomes too heavy?
o: It can become a bottleneck and actually slow down communication
It loses its address table and must relearn it
It automatically converts into a repeater
It begins broadcasting all frames to every segment
questions.e: Bridges work best where traffic between segments is not too great; when inter-segment traffic becomes heavy the bridge can become a bottleneck and slow communication down. Their forwarding decisions are also relatively low-level and simple compared with those of a router.

questions.q: A switch operates at which OSI layer, and which communication types does it support?
o: Layer 3, supporting only unicast
Layer 2, the data link layer, supporting unicast, multicast and broadcast
Layer 1, supporting broadcast only
Layer 4, supporting unicast and multicast
questions.e: A switch operates at layer 2, the data link layer, and supports unicast, multicast and broadcast communications. When a frame arrives at a port it examines the destination address, performs the necessary checks, and sends the frame to the corresponding device or devices.

questions.q: Routers operate at which layer and pass data between networks based on what information?
o: Layer 3, the network layer, based on network protocol or layer 3 information
Layer 2, based on MAC addresses
Layer 1, based on signal strength
Layer 7, based on application data
questions.e: Routers are internetworking devices operating at layer 3, the network layer, passing packets between networks based on network protocol or layer 3 information. They receive, analyze and forward packets and can make intelligent decisions about the best delivery path.

questions.q: In what ways may the heterogeneous networks interconnected by a router differ?
o: In physical characteristics, frame size, transmission rate, topologies and addressing
Only in physical characteristics and topology
Only in addressing scheme
Only in transmission rate
questions.e: Routers can interconnect two or more networks that are heterogeneous or homogenous, and heterogeneous networks may differ in physical characteristics, frame size, transmission rate, topologies and addressing. Reconciling these differences is why routers are described as intelligent devices with higher capabilities than repeaters and bridges.

questions.q: How many network interface cards does a router have?
o: One, shared across all connected networks
One per host on the attached networks
Always exactly two
The same number as the number of networks it connects to
questions.e: A router has the same number of NICs as the number of networks it connects to, effectively acting as a special host on more than one network. This is what allows multiple networks to be joined using one or more routers.

questions.q: Which network problem is specifically solved by using a router rather than a bridge?
o: Loss of synchronization between devices
Excessive broadcast traffic, since routers do not forward broadcast frames unless specifically told to
Signal attenuation over long distances
Incompatible cable types
questions.e: Routers solve the problem of excessive broadcast traffic because they do not forward broadcast frames unless specifically configured to do so. Signal attenuation is instead the problem a repeater addresses.

questions.q: A gateway is best described as which of the following?
o: A layer 2 device that filters frames by MAC address
A network node forming a passage between two networks operating with different transmission protocols
A multiport repeater at the center of a star network
A device that only regenerates weakened signals
questions.e: A gateway is a network node forming a passage between two networks that operate with different transmission protocols, acting as the entry and exit point through which all cross-network traffic must pass. It is a very powerful computer compared with a bridge or router, typically used to connect huge and incompatible networks.

questions.q: At which OSI layer does a gateway operate?
o: Always at layer 3
Only at layer 7
Most commonly at layer 3, but depending on functionality it can operate at any of the seven layers
Always at layer 2
questions.e: The most common type, the network gateway, operates at layer 3, but depending on its functionality a gateway can operate at any of the seven OSI layers. This flexibility is what allows it to bridge fundamentally incompatible networks.

questions.q: Which protocol is credited with hiding the details of the physical and data-link layers of different networks so that the entire Internet appears as a single network?
o: SMTP
IP
TCP
HDLC
questions.e: The IP protocol hides the details of the physical and data-link layers of different networks so that the whole Internet appears as a single network. The Internet is given as the popular example of an internetwork, a network of networks.

questions.q: What distinguishes the function of switching from that of routing?
o: Switching moves packets between different networks; routing moves them within one network
Switching moves data packets between devices on the same network or LAN; routing moves packets between different networks
Switching operates at layer 3 and routing at layer 2
Switching applies only to analog signals and routing only to digital
questions.e: Switching moves data packets between devices on the same network or LAN, while routing moves packets between different networks. This matches their layers: a switch works at the data link layer while a router works at the network layer.

questions.q: In the comparison of routers and switches, which statement is accurate about their usage and data format?
o: Both are used only in MANs and send only frames
Routers are used only in LANs and send frames; switches are used in LANs and MANs and send packets
Routers send frames only; switches send packets only
Routers are used in LAN and MAN and send data as packets; switches are used only in LAN and send data as packets and frames
questions.e: Routers are used in LAN and MAN environments and send data in the form of packets, whereas switches are used only in LAN environments and send data as packets and frames. Their routing and switching types also differ: adaptive and non-adaptive routing versus circuit, packet and message switching.

questions.q: In a switched communication network, what is the role of the nodes?
o: They convert data between analog and digital forms
They are not concerned with the content of the data, merely switching it from node to node
They generate the data being transmitted
They interpret the content of the data to decide its priority
questions.e: Nodes in a switched network are not concerned with the content of the data; data is simply routed by being switched from node to node. The end devices, called stations, are the computers, terminals and phones that originate and receive the data.

questions.q: Which three switching techniques are available for digital traffic?
o: Fixed, flooding and random switching
Datagram, virtual circuit and adaptive switching
Circuit switching, packet switching and message switching
Static, dynamic and default switching
questions.e: The three main switching techniques for digital traffic are circuit switching, packet switching and message switching. Datagram and virtual circuit are the two approaches within packet switching rather than separate top-level techniques.

questions.q: What are the three phases of circuit switching?
o: Setup, routing and teardown
Initialization, data transfer and disconnect
Establish, transfer and disconnect
Request, accept and terminate
questions.e: Circuit switching passes through establish, transfer and disconnect phases, also described as circuit establishment, data transfer and circuit disconnect. A complete end-to-end path must exist before communication can take place.

questions.q: When are routing decisions made in circuit switching?
o: Only when congestion is detected
When the circuit is first established, with no decisions made after that time
Independently for each packet as it arrives
At the end of the transfer, during teardown
questions.e: In circuit switching, routing decisions are made when the circuit is first established and none are made thereafter. This is why data can flow without further delay once the connection is complete and the destination has acknowledged readiness.

questions.q: Which is listed as a disadvantage of circuit switching?
o: The message must be stored in its entirety at each node
Each packet must carry a full destination address
Packets may arrive out of order
Inefficient use of the communication channel and longer connection establishment time
questions.e: Circuit switching requires more bandwidth, has a longer connection establishment time, is more expensive because a dedicated path is needed per connection, and uses the communication channel inefficiently. Out-of-order arrival is a datagram packet switching characteristic instead.

questions.q: In telecommunications terminology, what is the 'local loop' or subscriber loop?
o: The branch between two exchanges
The device attached to the network by the subscriber
The connection from the subscriber to the network, a few km up to a few tens of km
The switching center that supports subscribers
questions.e: The subscriber line, also called the local loop or subscriber loop, is the connection to the network and runs from a few kilometres up to a few tens of kilometres. Trunks are the different component: the branches between exchanges.

questions.q: In packet switching, how are messages handled and addressed?
o: Messages are broken into packets, each tagged with source and destination addresses, and individual packets may take different routes
The whole message travels as one unit with a single address
Messages travel over a dedicated reserved circuit
Messages are stored at each node before being forwarded whole
questions.e: In packet switching the message is broken into packets, each tagged with the appropriate source and destination address, and individual packets may take different routes to the destination. All packets are reassembled at the receiving end in the correct order.

questions.q: Datagram packet switching is also known by which name, and what is its defining characteristic?
o: Message switching, with store and forward at each node
Connectionless switching, with no fixed path and each packet treated independently
Circuit switching, with a dedicated path
Connection-oriented switching, with a preplanned route
questions.e: Datagram packet switching is also known as connectionless switching, and the path is not fixed: each packet is treated independently, may take any practical route, may arrive out of order and may go missing. It is up to the receiver to reorder packets and recover from any that are lost.

questions.q: In virtual circuit packet switching, what does each packet contain instead of a destination address?
o: A source route list
A sequence number only
A hop count
A virtual circuit identifier
questions.e: Each packet in virtual circuit switching contains a virtual circuit identifier rather than a full destination address, since a preplanned route is established before any packets are sent. Because the route is fixed in advance, no routing decision is needed for each individual packet.

questions.q: Virtual Circuit Switching is also known as which type of switching, and how is the connection set up?
o: Connection-oriented switching, with call request and call accept packets establishing the connection in a handshake
Dedicated switching, with resources permanently reserved
Connectionless switching, with no setup
Adaptive switching, with routes recalculated per packet
questions.e: Virtual circuit switching is connection-oriented, with call request and call accept packets establishing the connection through a handshake and a clear request used to drop the circuit. Importantly it is not a dedicated path, which distinguishes it from circuit switching.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts virtual circuits with datagrams?
o: Virtual circuits can provide sequencing and error control and forward packets more quickly, but are less reliable since loss of a node loses all circuits through it
Virtual circuits have no call setup phase; datagrams do
Datagrams are better when many packets are sent; virtual circuits are better for few packets
Datagrams provide sequencing and error control; virtual circuits do not
questions.e: Virtual circuits let the network provide sequencing and error control and forward packets more quickly since no routing decision is needed per packet, but they are less reliable because losing a node loses every circuit passing through it. Datagrams have no call setup phase, are better when only a few packets are sent, are more flexible, and allow routing around congested parts of the network.

questions.q: What distinguishes a connection-oriented path from a dedicated path?
o: Both reserve resources exclusively, differing only in duration

A connection-oriented path preplans the route but does not necessarily reserve resources, which may be shared; a dedicated path preplans the route and allocates resources to one sender and receiver only
Neither preplans the route
A connection-oriented path reserves all resources; a dedicated path shares them
questions.e: A connection-oriented path has a preplanned source-to-destination route but does not necessarily reserve resources, which other source-destination pairs may share; a dedicated path both preplans the route and allocates resources exclusively. Virtual circuit switching combines features of circuit and datagram switching by being connection-oriented without necessarily being dedicated.

questions.q: Message switching networks are described as which type of network, and why?
o: Reserved networks, because a path is dedicated in advance
Broadcast networks, because every node receives every message
Store and forward networks, because each node receives the entire message, stores it on disk, then transmits it to the next node
Cut-through networks, because nodes forward before fully receiving
questions.e: Message switching is a store and forward approach: each node receives the entire message, stores it in its entirety on disk, and then transmits it onward. No dedicated path between the two stations is needed, and the destination address is simply appended to the message.

questions.q: Which is a stated disadvantage of message switching?
o: Bandwidth cannot be shared among devices
Traffic congestion increases because nothing is buffered
Message priority cannot be used
Switches must have sufficient storage to hold messages until forwarded, and long delays can occur due to storing and forwarding
questions.e: Message switches must be equipped with enough storage to hold messages until forwarding, and long delays can result from the store-and-forward operation. Its advantages are the opposite of the other options: shared data channels improve bandwidth efficiency, buffering reduces congestion, and message priority can be used to manage the network.

questions.q: Routing is defined as which process?
o: Selecting a path for traffic between or across multiple networks
Assigning time slots to competing transmitters
Regenerating a weakened signal along a transmission path
Converting frames into packets at a network boundary
questions.e: Routing is the process of selecting a path for traffic between or across multiple networks. It is classified into static, default and dynamic categories.

questions.q: Static routing is also known by which name, and how are routes added?
o: Default routing, with all traffic sent to one next hop
Dynamic routing, with protocols exchanging updates
Nonadaptive routing, with the administrator manually adding routes to the routing table
Adaptive routing, with routes discovered automatically
questions.e: Static routing is also called nonadaptive routing, and the administrator manually adds the routes into the routing table. Routing decisions are therefore not made on the basis of network condition or topology.

questions.q: Which is listed as an advantage of static routing?
o: It consumes less bandwidth than default routing
No routing overhead for the router CPU, so a cheaper router can be used, and it adds security since only the administrator can allow routing to particular networks
It requires no knowledge of the topology
It automatically adapts when a route fails
questions.e: Static routing imposes no routing overhead on the router CPU, allowing cheaper hardware, and improves security because only the administrator can permit routing to particular networks. Its disadvantages are that manual configuration is laborious on large networks and demands that the administrator know the topology well.

questions.q: In default routing, what happens when a specific route to a destination is present in the routing table?
o: The packet is dropped as ambiguous
Both routes are used alternately to balance load
The default route is always preferred for consistency
The router chooses the specific route rather than the default route
questions.e: When a specific route is mentioned in the routing table the router chooses it rather than the default route; the default is used only when no specific route exists. Default routing suits networks with a single exit point or where the bulk of traffic goes to the same next hop device.

questions.q: Which protocols are named as the best examples of dynamic routing protocols?
o: SMTP and FTP
TCP and UDP
HDLC and LLC
RIP and OSPF
questions.e: RIP and OSPF are given as the best examples of dynamic routing protocols. Dynamic routing makes automatic adjustments according to the current state of routes, using protocols to discover network destinations and the paths to reach them.

questions.q: Which is listed as a disadvantage of dynamic routing?
o: It consumes more bandwidth for communicating with neighbours and is less secure than static routing
It requires the administrator to know the entire topology
It cannot recover when a route goes down
It is difficult to configure
questions.e: Dynamic routing consumes more bandwidth communicating with neighbouring routers and is less secure than static routing. It is actually easy to configure and more effective at selecting the best route and discovering remote networks, which are its advantages.

questions.q: In routing for circuit switched networks, what do the two requirements of efficiency and resilience mean?
o: Efficiency is minimising hop count; resilience is maximising bandwidth
Efficiency is handling the expected traffic load with the smallest amount of equipment; resilience is handling surges of traffic that exceed the expected load
Efficiency is reducing latency; resilience is encrypting traffic
Efficiency is using static routes; resilience is using dynamic routes
questions.e: Efficiency is the ability to handle the expected load of traffic using the smallest amount of equipment, while resilience is the ability to handle surges of traffic exceeding that expected load. Public telephone switches use a tree structure, with dynamic routing employing a peer structure for nodes.

questions.q: In alternate routing, how are the possible routes handled?
o: Possible routes between end offices are predefined and listed in preference order, with the originating switch selecting the appropriate one
Only a single permanent route exists per pair
All routes are used simultaneously to spread load
Routes are computed fresh for each call
questions.e: In alternate routing the possible routes between end offices are predefined and listed in preference order, and the originating switch selects the appropriate route. Different sets of routes may be used at different times.

questions.q: Which characteristic required of packet-switched routing refers to being adaptive to changes of network topology and varying traffic load?
o: Correctness
Cleverness
Robustness
Efficiency
questions.e: Robustness is adaptiveness to changes in network topology and varying traffic load. Cleverness is the separate ability to detour congested links and determine network connectivity, while efficiency concerns rapid route finding and minimising control messages.

questions.q: Which two performance criteria are used for route selection?
o: Highest reliability and lowest jitter
Shortest queue and fewest collisions
Minimum hop and least cost
Maximum bandwidth and minimum latency
questions.e: Route selection uses minimum hop and least cost as its performance criteria. Least cost is the more general of the two, since minimum hop is simply the special case where each link is assigned a cost of 1.

questions.q: Which four routing strategies are identified?
o: Unicast, multicast, broadcast and anycast
Fixed, flooding, random and adaptive
Static, default, dynamic and hybrid
Circuit, packet, message and virtual
questions.e: The four routing strategies are fixed, flooding, random and adaptive. Fixed uses a single permanent route per source-destination pair, while adaptive changes decisions as network conditions change.

questions.q: In fixed routing, what is created and where is it stored, and what is the drawback?
o: A central routing matrix based on least-cost paths, stored in the network control center; the drawback is that if the control center fails everything collapses
A distance vector table at each router; the drawback is slow convergence
A cache of recent routes at each switch; the drawback is stale entries
A flooding table at each node; the drawback is duplicate packets
questions.e: Fixed routing builds a central routing matrix based on least-cost paths, stored in the network control center, showing for each source-destination pair the identity of the next node on the route. Its drawback is a single point of failure: if the network control center fails, everything collapses, so it is not reliable.

questions.q: In flooding, how are incoming packets handled?
o: They are retransmitted on all links including the incoming one
They are forwarded on a single randomly chosen link
They are retransmitted on every link except the incoming link
They are held until a least-cost route is computed
questions.e: In flooding a packet is sent by a node to every neighbour, with incoming packets retransmitted on every link except the one they arrived on. No network information is required at all for this strategy.

questions.q: How are duplicate packets controlled in a flooding scheme?
o: Each packet carries a checksum that changes on each hop
Each packet is uniquely numbered so duplicates can be discarded, nodes remember packets already forwarded, and a hop count can be included
Duplicates are impossible because each link is used once
Each node forwards only the first packet it ever receives
questions.e: Duplicates are managed by uniquely numbering each packet so copies can be discarded, having nodes remember which packets they already forwarded, and optionally including a hop count in packets. These measures keep the network load within bounds despite the inherent duplication.

questions.q: Which property of flooding guarantees that the fastest possible delivery occurs?
o: It selects the least cost route by computation
It uses adaptive feedback from congested nodes
Because all possible routes are tried, at least one packet will have taken the minimum hop count route
It reserves bandwidth in advance along every path
questions.e: Because flooding tries all possible routes, at least one packet is guaranteed to have travelled the minimum hop count route. Flooding is also very robust and visits all nodes, making it useful for distributing information such as routing data, and suited to emergency or military messages.

questions.q: In random routing, how is the outgoing path chosen and what is the consequence for route quality?
o: By least-cost computation, so the route is optimal
Randomly or by round robin, possibly using a probability calculation, so the route is typically neither least cost nor minimum hop
By consulting a central matrix, so the route is always minimum hop
By flooding all links then selecting the fastest reply
questions.e: In random routing a node selects one outgoing path for retransmission, chosen randomly or by round robin, possibly based on a probability calculation, and no network information is needed. The resulting route is typically neither least cost nor minimum hop.

questions.q: Adaptive routing is used by almost all packet switching networks. What conditions cause its routing decisions to change?
o: Failure and congestion
Changes in the number of attached hosts
Changes in cable type and frame size
Time of day only
questions.e: Adaptive routing changes its decisions as network conditions change, specifically in response to failure and congestion. It requires information about the network, creating a tradeoff between the quality of that information and the overhead of collecting it.

questions.q: What is the stated advantage and disadvantage of adaptive routing?
o: Advantage: guaranteed minimum hop; Disadvantage: requires a central control center
Advantage: no network information required; Disadvantage: routes are rarely optimal
Advantage: lowest possible overhead; Disadvantage: cannot respond to failures
Advantage: improved performance and a tendency to balance loads; Disadvantage: the routing decision is more complex, increasing the processing burden on network nodes
questions.e: Adaptive routing improves performance and tends to balance loads, but its routing decisions are more complex, increasing the processing burden on network nodes. It is more complex than non-adaptive algorithms and is the approach used by dynamic routing.

questions.q: How is the cost of a path between two nodes defined in a least cost algorithm?
o: The number of links traversed, regardless of their weights
The maximum single link cost along the path
The sum of the costs of the links traversed
The average of the link costs along the path
questions.e: The cost of a path between two nodes is the sum of the costs of the links traversed, and for each pair of nodes the goal is to find a path with the least such cost. Minimum hop routing is the special case in which every link is given a cost of 1.

questions.q: In least cost routing, what is noted about link costs in opposite directions?
o: They are always inversely proportional to each other
They must always be identical for the algorithm to work
They may be different, for example reflecting the length of the packet queue
They are undefined for bi-directional links
questions.e: Link costs in different directions may be different, with the length of the packet queue given as an example of a directional cost measure. A link value may also be set inversely proportional to capacity, so that higher capacity links appear cheaper.

questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in what manner?
o: From a given source node to all other nodes, developing paths in order of increasing path length
From a given source to a single specified destination only
By relaxing every edge n−1 times regardless of order
From all nodes to all other nodes simultaneously
