questions.e: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a given source node to all other nodes, developing paths in order of increasing path length. Relaxing every edge n−1 times is the method of the Bellman-Ford algorithm instead.

questions.q: In the notation for Dijkstra's algorithm, what does w(i, j) equal when two nodes are not directly connected?
o: Infinity
The number of intermediate hops
Zero
One
questions.e: The link cost w(i, j) is infinity when the two nodes are not directly connected, is 0 when i equals j, and is non-negative when they are directly connected. Setting non-adjacent pairs to infinity ensures they are never selected before a real path is found.

questions.q: In the initialization step of Dijkstra's algorithm, what are T and L(n) set to?
o: T = the empty set, and L(n) = 0 for all n
T = all nodes, and L(n) = infinity for all n
T = {s}, and L(n) = infinity for all n including s
T = {s}, containing only the source node, and L(n) = w(s, n) for n not equal to s
questions.e: Initialization sets T = {s}, so the set of incorporated nodes contains only the source, and L(n) = w(s, n) for n ≠ s, meaning initial path costs to neighbouring nodes are simply the link costs. The algorithm then repeatedly adds the nearest node not yet in T.

questions.q: What is the update formula used in step 3 of Dijkstra's algorithm?
o: L(n) = min[L(n), L(x) + w(x, n)] for all n not in T
L(n) = max[L(n), L(x) + w(x, n)] for all n in T
L(n) = L(x) + w(x, n) for all n
L(n) = min[L(n), w(s, n)] for all n
questions.e: The update step computes L(n) = min[L(n), L(x) + w(x, n)] for all nodes n not yet in T; if the latter term is the minimum, the path from s to n is the path from s to x concatenated with the edge from x to n. One iteration of steps 2 and 3 adds exactly one new node to T.

questions.q: When does Dijkstra's algorithm terminate, and what does the value L(x) represent at that point?
o: After n−1 relaxations; L(x) is an upper bound on the distance to x
When all nodes have been added to T; L(x) is the cost of the least-cost path from s to x
When the source's neighbours are all visited; L(x) is the hop count to x
When no negative weights remain; L(x) is the average path cost
questions.e: The algorithm terminates when all nodes have been added to T, at which point L(x) is the cost of the least-cost path from s to each node x, and T itself defines those least-cost paths. Terminating after n−1 relaxations is characteristic of Bellman-Ford.

questions.q: In the step-by-step description of Dijkstra's algorithm, how is the current node C chosen at each stage?
o: A randomly selected non-visited node
The visited node with the largest current distance
The node adjacent to the most neighbours
The non-visited node with the smallest current distance
questions.e: At each stage the non-visited node with the smallest current distance is set as the current node C. Its neighbours are then examined, adding C's current distance to the connecting edge weight and updating a neighbour's distance if the result is smaller.

questions.q: In a worked Dijkstra example with nodes A to G and source A, the first pass selects A and updates its neighbours B and C, producing dist = {0, 5, 6, ∞, ∞, ∞, ∞}. Which node is selected in pass 2, and why?
o: Node D, because it is adjacent to the most nodes
Node G, because it is furthest from the source
Node B, because it has the lowest dist value of 5 among the remaining nodes
Node C, because it has the largest finite distance
questions.e: Pass 2 selects node B because it has the lowest dist value of 5 among the nodes still in Q. Its neighbours C, D and E are then updated, giving dist = {0, 5, 6, 12, 13, ∞, ∞}.

questions.q: Continuing that example, after pass 3 selects node C the distances become {0, 5, 6, 8, 13, 10, ∞}. What does the change in D's value from 12 to 8 demonstrate?
o: That node D must be removed from the graph
That the algorithm has detected a negative weight cycle
That a node's tentative distance can be improved when a shorter path through a newly added node is found
That node D was incorrectly initialised
questions.e: D's tentative distance falls from 12 to 8 because reaching D via C proves cheaper than the earlier path via B, which is exactly what the update rule L(n) = min[L(n), L(x) + w(x, n)] is designed to capture. Tentative distances are therefore upper bounds that shrink until the node is finalised.

questions.q: In that worked example, pass 5 finds two nodes tied with the lowest dist value of 10. How is the tie resolved?
o: The algorithm halts and reports an ambiguity
The node with more neighbours is chosen
Both nodes are added to S simultaneously
Either node may be selected, and one is chosen arbitrarily
questions.e: When nodes E and F are tied at a dist value of 10, either one may be selected and one is chosen arbitrarily, with E taken in the worked example. The final result is unaffected, since the other tied node is selected on the following pass.

questions.q: The Bellman-Ford algorithm proceeds by finding shortest paths subject to what kind of constraint?
o: Paths containing at most one link, then at most two links, and so on
Paths visiting each node exactly once
Paths of exactly n links, where n is the node count
Paths with no repeated edge weights
questions.e: Bellman-Ford first finds shortest paths from the given node subject to the constraint that paths contain at most one link, then at most two links, and so on. The quantity Lh(n) denotes the cost of the least-cost path from s to n under the constraint of no more than h links.

questions.q: What is the update formula in the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
o: Lh+1(n) = Lh(n) + w(s, n)
Lh+1(n) = min[Lh(n), w(s, n)]
Lh+1(n) = max[Lh(j) + w(j, n)]
Lh+1(n) = min[Lh(j) + w(j, n)]
questions.e: The update computes Lh+1(n) = min[Lh(j) + w(j, n)], connecting n with the predecessor node j that achieves the minimum and eliminating any connection to a different predecessor formed in an earlier iteration. If the previous path is shorter it is retained; otherwise a new path is defined.

questions.q: In the initialization of Bellman-Ford, what values are assigned?
o: L0(n) = 1 for all n, and Lh(s) = 0
L0(n) = infinity for all n not equal to s, and Lh(s) = 0 for all h
L0(n) = w(s, n) for all n, and Lh(s) = infinity
L0(n) = 0 for all n, and Lh(s) = infinity for all h
questions.e: Initialization sets L0(n) = ∞ for all n other than the source, and Lh(s) = 0 for all values of h. The source's cost to itself is zero at every stage, while all other nodes start unreachable.

questions.q: Which three differences between Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra are stated?
o: Bellman-Ford works only on undirected graphs while Dijkstra works on directed graphs
Bellman-Ford requires a central control center while Dijkstra does not

Bellman-Ford relaxes n−1 times while Dijkstra relaxes once, Bellman-Ford handles negative weights while Dijkstra cannot, and Bellman-Ford visits a vertex more than once while Dijkstra visits it only once
Bellman-Ford is faster, uses less memory, and handles more nodes
questions.e: Bellman-Ford performs relaxation n−1 times whereas Dijkstra does so once, Bellman-Ford can handle negative weights whereas Dijkstra cannot, and Bellman-Ford may visit a vertex more than once whereas Dijkstra visits each only once. These properties are why Bellman-Ford is the more time consuming of the two.

questions.q: In the Bellman-Ford relaxation step, under what condition is d(v) updated?
o: If c(u, v) is negative
If d(u) + c(u, v) is greater than d(v)
If v has not yet been visited
If d(u) + c(u, v) is less than d(v)
questions.e: Relaxation means that if d(u) + c(u, v) < d(v), then d(v) is set to d(u) + c(u, v). This test is applied to every edge on every iteration, which is why the algorithm can correct distances it had previously set.

questions.q: For a Bellman-Ford example on a graph with 6 vertices, how many iterations are performed, and what happens if more are run?
o: Six iterations; running more improves accuracy
Five iterations; running more produces no change in the distances
Five iterations; running more detects extra shortest paths
Six iterations; running more produces an error
questions.e: With 6 vertices the algorithm relaxes all edges 5 times, that is n−1 iterations, and if the loop runs more than 5 times the answer remains the same with no change in the distances between vertices. Convergence after n−1 rounds is guaranteed in the absence of a negative weight cycle.

questions.q: In a Bellman-Ford example, edge (A, C) gives vertex C a distance of 4, but later edge (D, C) with d(D) = 5 and weight −2 is examined. What happens to C's distance?
o: It is updated to 3, because 5 − 2 is less than 4
It stays at 4, because 4 is already smaller
It becomes infinite, because negative weights are rejected
It is updated to 7, because 5 + 2 exceeds 4
questions.e: Since d(D) + c(D, C) = 5 − 2 = 3 is less than the current value 4, the distance of vertex C is updated to 3. This ability to lower an already-assigned distance using a negative edge is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm cannot do.

questions.q: Why are negative weight edges described as useful rather than merely a curiosity?
o: Because they make Dijkstra's algorithm run faster
Because they reduce the number of iterations required
Because they guarantee a unique shortest path
Because they can model phenomena such as cashflow or heat absorbed and released in chemical reactions
questions.e: Negative weights can represent real phenomena such as cashflow, or heat released and absorbed in chemical reactions, where heat absorption is modelled as negative weight and dissipation as positive. This lets a shortest-path search find the set of reactions requiring minimum energy.

questions.q: What are the stated time complexities of Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra's algorithms?
o: O(V^2) for both
O(E log V) for Bellman-Ford and O(VE) for Dijkstra
O(V + E) for Bellman-Ford and O(V^2) for Dijkstra
O(VE) for Bellman-Ford and O(E log V) for Dijkstra
questions.e: Bellman-Ford has time complexity O(VE) and Dijkstra has O(E log V), making Bellman-Ford the more time consuming and higher-overhead of the two. Bellman-Ford compensates by handling negative weight edges and detecting negative weight cycles.

questions.q: Which algorithm is described as easily implemented in a distributed way, and what does each algorithm's result contain?
o: Bellman-Ford is easily distributed, and its result contains vertices with information about the other vertices they are connected to, whereas Dijkstra's result contains whole-network information
Dijkstra is easily distributed; its result contains only the vertices it connects to
Neither can be distributed; both produce identical results
Both are equally easy to distribute, differing only in speed
questions.e: Bellman-Ford can easily be implemented in a distributed way while Dijkstra's algorithm cannot. Bellman-Ford's result gives each vertex information about the vertices it is connected to, whereas Dijkstra's result contains whole-network information rather than just immediate connections.

questions.q: An IPv4 address is defined as an address of what length, identifying what?
o: 64 bits, identifying a physical network interface card
32 bits, uniquely and universally defining the connection of a device to the Internet
128 bits, identifying a host and its subnet
16 bits, identifying a network only
questions.e: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long and uniquely and universally defines the connection of a device, such as a computer or router, to the Internet. The 128-bit length belongs to IPv6, which was introduced to address IPv4 address depletion.

questions.q: What is the size of the IPv4 address space?
questions.e: The IPv4 address space is 2^32, that is 4,294,967,296 addresses, because the address is 32 bits long. IPv4 addresses may be written in binary notation or dotted-decimal notation.

questions.q: An IP address is best described as which of the following?
o: A device that divides traffic into packets for transport
A set of rules dictating how data should be delivered over the Internet
An identifying number associated with a specific computer or computer network, allowing it to send and receive information when connected to the Internet
A mask used to separate the network portion from the host portion
questions.e: An IP address is an identifying number associated with a specific computer or computer network, allowing computers to send and receive information when connected to the Internet. The set of rules dictating how data is delivered is the Internet Protocol itself, which works alongside TCP to divide traffic into packets.

questions.q: Convert the binary IPv4 address 10000001 00001011 00001011 11101111 into dotted-decimal notation.
questions.e: Replacing each group of 8 bits with its decimal equivalent and inserting dots gives 129.11.11.239. Applying the same method to 11000001 10000011 00011011 11111111 yields 193.131.27.255.

questions.q: Convert the dotted-decimal address 221.34.7.82 into binary notation.
questions.e: Replacing each decimal number with its 8-bit binary equivalent gives 11011101 00100010 00000111 01010010. The address 111.56.45.78 converts by the same method to 01101111 00111000 00101101 01001110.

questions.q: What is the error in the IPv4 address 111.56.045.78?
o: There must be no leading zero, so 045 is invalid
Binary and dotted-decimal notation have been mixed
There are more than four numbers
A number exceeds 255
questions.e: The address 111.56.045.78 is invalid because there must be no leading zero, making 045 illegal. The other classic errors are exceeding four numbers, a value greater than 255, and mixing binary with dotted-decimal notation.

questions.q: What is the error in the IPv4 address 75.45.301.14?
o: A leading zero is present
There are more than four numbers
Binary and dotted-decimal notation have been mixed
Each number must be less than or equal to 255, and 301 exceeds this
questions.e: Each number in a dotted-decimal IPv4 address must be less than or equal to 255, so 301 is invalid. The address 221.34.7.8.20 fails a different rule, having more than four numbers.

questions.q: What is the error in the address 11100010.23.14.67?
o: A leading zero is present
There are more than four numbers
A number exceeds 255
A mixture of binary notation and dotted-decimal notation is not allowed
questions.e: Mixing binary notation with dotted-decimal notation within one address is not allowed, which is the fault in 11100010.23.14.67. Each address must be written consistently in one notation or the other.

questions.q: In classful addressing, the address space is divided into how many classes, and which are they?
o: Two classes: unicast and multicast
Five classes: A, B, C, D and E
Four classes: A, B, C and D
Three classes: A, B and C
questions.e: Classful addressing divides the address space into five classes: A, B, C, D and E. Classes A, B and C are used for unicast, class D for multicast and class E is reserved.

questions.q: In binary notation, which leading bit pattern identifies a class C address?
questions.e: A class C address begins with the bits 110. Class A begins with 0, class B with 10, class D with 1110 and class E with 1111.

questions.q: An address begins 11000001 10000011 00011011 11111111. What is its class, and why?
o: Class B, because the first bit is 1 and the second is 0
Class E, because the first four bits are 1
Class C, because the first two bits are 1 and the third bit is 0
Class A, because the first bit is 0
questions.e: The first two bits are 1 and the third bit is 0, giving the pattern 110, which identifies a class C address. By contrast an address beginning with a 0 bit, such as 00000001 00001011 00001011 11101111, is class A.

questions.q: In dotted-decimal notation, which first-byte range identifies a class A address?
questions.e: A first byte in the range 0-127 identifies a class A address, which is why 14.23.120.8 is class A. The range 192-223 identifies class C, 224-239 class D and 240-255 class E.

questions.q: The address 252.5.15.111 belongs to which class?
o: Class C
Class E
Class B
Class D
questions.e: The first byte is 252, which falls in the 240-255 range identifying class E. Class D covers first bytes 224-239 and is used for multicast, while class E is reserved.

questions.q: In the classful block structure, how many blocks exist in class A and what is each block's size?
o: 1 block of 268,435,456 addresses
128 blocks of 16,777,216 addresses each
16,384 blocks of 65,536 addresses each
2,097,152 blocks of 256 addresses each
questions.e: Class A has 128 blocks, each containing 16,777,216 addresses, and is used for unicast. Class B has 16,384 blocks of 65,536 addresses and class C has 2,097,152 blocks of 256 addresses, both also unicast.

questions.q: How many addresses does each class C block contain, and what is class C used for?
o: 256 addresses, used for unicast
268,435,456 addresses, reserved
65,536 addresses, used for multicast
16,777,216 addresses, used for unicast
questions.e: Each class C block contains 256 addresses and class C is used for unicast, with 2,097,152 such blocks available. The 268,435,456-address figure applies to classes D and E, each of which forms a single block used for multicast and reserved purposes respectively.

questions.q: What are the default masks for classes A, B and C in CIDR notation?
o: /16, /24 and /32 respectively
/8, /16 and /24 respectively
/24, /16 and /8 respectively
/4, /8 and /12 respectively
questions.e: The default masks are /8 for class A (255.0.0.0), /16 for class B (255.255.0.0) and /24 for class C (255.255.255.0). Each mask is a 32-bit number of contiguous 1s followed by contiguous 0s, used to separate the net ID from the host ID.

questions.q: The dotted-decimal mask 255.255.0.0 corresponds to which class and which CIDR notation?
o: Class A, /8
Class B, /16
Class D, /32
Class C, /24
questions.e: The mask 255.255.0.0 is the class B default, written /16, and in binary it is 11111111 11111111 00000000 00000000. Class A uses 255.0.0.0 (/8) and class C uses 255.255.255.0 (/24).

questions.q: An IPv4 address is structured into which two parts, and what helps identify them?
o: Net ID and Host ID, identified using a mask of contiguous 1s followed by contiguous 0s
Network address and broadcast address, identified by position in the block
Prefix and suffix, identified by the leading bit pattern
Source ID and Destination ID, identified by the routing table
questions.e: An IPv4 address consists of a Net ID and a Host ID, and a mask — a 32-bit number of contiguous 1s followed by contiguous 0s — is used to find where the boundary between them falls. The mask is what makes the two-level hierarchy operationally usable.

questions.q: What is the difference between subnetting and supernetting?
o: Subnetting combines blocks into a larger space; supernetting divides them into smaller groups
Subnetting applies to class A only; supernetting applies to class C only
Subnetting divides a large address block into smaller sub-groups; supernetting combines several contiguous address spaces into a larger single address space
Both divide blocks, differing only in whether the mask is flexible
questions.e: Subnetting divides a large address block into smaller sub-groups using a flexible net mask, while supernetting combines several contiguous address spaces into a single larger one. Supernetting arose because the class A and B address spaces were exhausted while demand for class B space remained huge.

questions.q: Which criticism motivates the move away from classful addressing?
o: It cannot support multicast traffic
It requires masks longer than 32 bits
It wastes a large part of the address space
It cannot be written in dotted-decimal notation
questions.e: Classful addressing wastes a large part of the address space, which is why classless addressing was introduced to overcome address depletion. The rigid block sizes of 16,777,216, 65,536 and 256 addresses rarely match an organization's actual needs.

questions.q: Which three restrictions apply to a block of addresses in classless addressing?
o: The block must lie entirely within one class, must not exceed 65,536 addresses, and must use a default mask
The addresses must be contiguous, the number of addresses must be a power of 2, and the first address must be evenly divisible by the number of addresses
The addresses must be non-contiguous, the count must be even, and the mask must be /24 or longer
The addresses must be sequential, the block size must be a multiple of 256, and the first address must end in zero
questions.e: In classless addressing the addresses in a block must be contiguous, the number of addresses must be a power of 2, and the first address must be evenly divisible by the number of addresses. The mask consists of n consecutive 1s followed by zeros, where n may be any number between 0 and 32.

questions.q: In the notation x.y.z.t/n used for a block of addresses, what do the two parts signify?
o: x.y.z.t is the network address and /n is the number of hosts
x.y.z.t defines one of the addresses in the block and /n defines the mask
x.y.z.t is the broadcast address and /n is the block count
x.y.z.t is the first address and /n is the last octet
questions.e: In the notation x.y.z.t/n, the dotted-decimal part defines one of the addresses in the block — not necessarily the first — and /n defines the mask. The first address is then found by setting the rightmost 32 − n bits to 0.

questions.q: Given the address 205.16.37.39/28, what is the first address in the block?
questions.e: Writing the address in binary as 11001101 00010000 00100101 00100111 and setting the rightmost 32 − 28 = 4 bits to 0 gives 11001101 00010000 00100101 00100000, that is 205.16.37.32. The first address is found by zeroing the host bits, not by rounding down to the nearest octet boundary.

questions.q: For the block containing 205.16.37.39/28, what is the last address?
questions.e: Setting the rightmost 32 − 28 = 4 bits to 1 gives 11001101 00010000 00100101 00101111, that is 205.16.37.47. The last address is obtained by setting all host bits to 1, mirroring the zeroing used for the first address.

questions.q: How many addresses are in the block defined by 205.16.37.39/28?
questions.e: The number of addresses is 2^(32 − n), and with n = 28 this gives 2^4 = 16 addresses. The value 28 is the prefix length rather than a count, so it must be subtracted from 32 before exponentiation.

questions.q: For a classless block, which formula gives the number of addresses it contains?
questions.e: The number of addresses in a block with mask /n is 2^(32 − n), since 32 − n bits remain available to identify hosts. A /28 block therefore holds 2^4 = 16 addresses, while a /24 block holds 2^8 = 256.

questions.q: In classless addressing, what values may the mask length n take?
o: Any number between 1 and 31
Only values that are powers of 2
Only 8, 16 or 24
Any number between 0 and 32
questions.e: The classless mask consists of n consecutive 1s followed by zeros, where n can be any number between 0 and 32. Restricting n to 8, 16 or 24 would reproduce the rigid class A, B and C boundaries that classless addressing was designed to escape.

questions.q: In a block of IPv4 addresses, how is the first address normally used?
o: It is used for loopback testing
It is assigned to the default gateway
It is reserved for broadcasting to all devices
It is not assigned to any device but serves as the network address representing the organization
questions.e: The first address in a block is normally not assigned to any device; it is used as the network address representing the organization to the rest of the world. The last address in the block is the broadcast address, used for broadcasting to all devices under the network.

questions.q: Given an address and its mask, how is the first address of the block calculated?
o: By ANDing the given address with the complement of the mask
By ORing the given address with the mask
By adding the mask to the given address
By ANDing the given address with the mask, bit by bit
questions.e: The first address is found by ANDing the given address with the mask bit by bit, where the result of ANDing two bits is 1 only if both are 1. The last address is found instead by ORing the address with the complement of the mask.

questions.q: How is the last address of a block found from an address and its mask?
o: By ANDing the address with the mask
By ORing the address with the mask itself
By ORing the address with the complement of the mask, where the complement is found by changing each 1 to 0 and each 0 to 1
By subtracting the mask from the address
questions.e: The last address is found by ORing the given address with the complement of the mask, bit by bit, where ORing two bits gives 0 only if both are 0. The complement is obtained by changing each 1 to 0 and each 0 to 1.

questions.q: How is the number of addresses in a block determined from the mask?
o: By counting the 1s in the mask
By dividing 2^32 by the mask value
By complementing the mask, interpreting the result as a decimal number, and adding 1
By subtracting the mask from 255.255.255.255
questions.e: The number of addresses is found by complementing the mask, interpreting it as a decimal number, and adding 1 to it. For example a /28 mask written in binary is twenty-eight 1s followed by four 0s.

questions.q: In the two-level hierarchical structure of an IPv4 address with prefix length n, what do the two parts define?
o: The leftmost n bits define the host and the rightmost 32 − n bits define the network
Both halves define the network, with the host identified separately
The leftmost 32 − n bits define the network and the rightmost n bits define the host
The leftmost n bits define the network and the rightmost 32 − n bits define the host
questions.e: Each address is a two-level hierarchy in which the leftmost n bits, the prefix, define the network, and the rightmost 32 − n bits define the host. Subnetting extends this into a three-level hierarchy.

questions.q: How many addresses does a router have, and what are they for?
o: Three: one per interface plus a management address
Two: one through which the device inside the router can be accessed, and another belonging to the granted block or sub-network
One per host on the attached sub-network
One, shared between the internal device and the network
questions.e: A router has two addresses: one through which the device inside the router can be accessed, and another belonging to the granted block or sub-network. This reflects the router's position straddling the boundary between the Internet and the sub-network.

questions.q: An ISP is granted 190.100.0.0/16, giving 65,536 addresses. If a customer needs 256 addresses, what prefix length is required?
questions.e: Since 256 addresses require log2 256 = 8 bits to define each host, the prefix length is 32 − 8 = 24. Customers needing 128 addresses require 7 host bits giving /25, and those needing 64 addresses require 6 host bits giving /26.

questions.q: In that ISP example, 65,536 addresses are granted and 40,960 are allocated across three customer groups. How many addresses remain available?
questions.e: Subtracting the 40,960 allocated addresses from the 65,536 granted leaves 24,576 addresses still available. The allocations comprised 64 customers with 256 addresses each, 128 customers with 128 each, and 128 customers with 64 each.

questions.q: Network Address Translation is defined as which process?
o: Dividing a network into subnets using a longer prefix
Converting a domain name into an IP address
Encrypting IP addresses to conceal internal topology
Translating one or more local IP addresses into one or more global IP addresses and vice versa, to provide Internet access to local hosts
questions.e: NAT translates one or more local IP addresses into one or more global IP addresses and back again, so that local hosts can reach the Internet. The core idea is to allow multiple devices to access the Internet through a single public address.

questions.q: Which is listed as a benefit of NAT?
o: Use of a single IP address among many devices in a network, and use of a dynamic IP address for home users for sharing
Elimination of the need for routing tables
Guaranteed quality of service for local hosts
Automatic encryption of all outbound traffic
questions.e: The benefits of NAT are the use of a single IP address among many devices in a network and the use of a dynamic IP address for home users for sharing, together with the use of private addresses internally. Only one public IP address is needed to access the Internet while private addresses are used within the network.

questions.q: What is the fundamental motivation for IPv6?
o: Address depletion remaining a long-term problem for the Internet, along with other problems in the IP protocol itself
The requirement to support wireless networks
The obsolescence of hexadecimal notation
The need for faster routing hardware
questions.e: Despite short-term solutions, address depletion remains a long-term problem for the Internet, and this together with other problems in the IP protocol itself motivated IPv6. The growing number of Internet hosts would eventually consume the entire IPv4 address space.

questions.q: Why is the theoretical IPv4 address space of 2^32 nodes described as largely wasted?
o: Because most addresses are reserved for broadcasting
Because routers cannot store that many entries
Because half the space is reserved for private use
Because of assignment inefficiencies, to which dividing the space into classes A, B and C contributed
questions.e: The theoretical address space of 2^32 nodes is largely wasted due to assignment inefficiencies, and dividing the address space into classes A, B and C made its own contribution to that inefficiency. This is why IPng was designed with a hierarchical address structure instead.

questions.q: What is the length of an IPv6 address, and how does it compare with IPv4?
o: 96 bits, tripled from IPv4's 32 bits
128 bits, increased from IPv4's 32 bits
64 bits, doubled from IPv4's 32 bits
256 bits, increased from IPv4's 64 bits
questions.e: An IPv6 address is 128 bits long, or 16 bytes, increased from the 32 bits of IPv4. This supports a far greater number of nodes with more levels of addressing hierarchy and simpler auto-configuration, even allowing for assignment inefficiency.

questions.q: IPv6 addresses are written using which notation?
o: Dotted decimal notation
Hexadecimal colon notation, with abbreviation permitted
Base-64 notation
Binary octet notation
questions.e: IPv6 uses hexadecimal colon notation, and addresses may be abbreviated, for instance by using a double colon to replace a run of zeros. Expanding an abbreviated address requires aligning the parts either side of the double colon to determine how many zeros it replaced.

questions.q: What is stated about the transition from IPv4 to IPv6?
o: It can only be performed by Internet service providers
It will be simple and flexible, with incremental upgrades and hosts able to keep their current addresses
It requires all existing addresses to be reassigned
It must be completed simultaneously across all hosts
questions.e: The transition is described as simple and flexible, with the upgrade being incremental so existing IPv4 hosts and routers may be upgraded and new ones installed independently, and upgraded hosts can continue using their current address. Start-up costs are low and little work is needed to upgrade existing systems.

questions.q: In the structure of an IPv6 address, what is the type prefix used for and what property must it have?
o: It stores the checksum, and must be recomputed at each hop
It defines the subnet mask, and must be contiguous
It is used for categorization, has variable length, and must have no partial conflict among the different prefixes
It identifies the host, and must be a fixed 16 bits
questions.e: The type prefix is used for categorization, is of variable length, and must have no partial conflict among the different prefixes. The no-partial-conflict requirement is what allows prefixes of differing lengths to be distinguished unambiguously.

questions.q: Which characteristics are attributed to IPv4 rather than IPv6 in the comparison of the two?
o: Support for quality of service, and being ideal for neighbouring node interaction
Being a connectionless protocol requiring less memory, with ease of remembering addresses, already supported by millions of devices
Hierarchical addressing and routing infrastructure, and stateful and stateless configuration
A 128-bit address space with simpler auto-configuration
questions.e: IPv4 is characterised as a connectionless protocol that allows a simple virtual communication layer over diversified devices, requires less memory, offers ease of remembering addresses, is already supported by millions of devices, and offers video libraries and conferences. Hierarchical addressing, stateful and stateless configuration, QoS support and suitability for neighbouring node interaction are attributed to IPv6.

questions.q: Which capability is listed for IPv6 but not for IPv4?
o: Support for quality of service (QoS)
Support by millions of existing devices
Connectionless operation
Ease of remembering addresses
questions.e: Support for quality of service is listed among IPv6's capabilities, alongside hierarchical addressing and routing infrastructure, stateful and stateless configuration, and suitability for neighbouring node interaction. Connectionless operation, ease of remembering addresses and broad existing device support are attributed to IPv4.

questions.q: What does 'IPng' stand for, and why was the naming significant?
o: Internet Protocol next generation, reflecting that changing the addressing scheme concerns all Internet users and offered an opportunity to add functionality
Internet Packet next group, reflecting its packet structure
Internet Protocol new gateway, reflecting its routing focus
Internet Protocol node grouping, reflecting its hierarchy
questions.e: IPng stands for 'Internet Protocol: The Next Generation'. Changing the IP addressing scheme was a matter concerning all Internet users and was therefore treated as an opportunity to provide additional functionality to IP, with most users agreeing it should have a hierarchical address structure.

questions.q: To access the Internet from a private network using NAT, what is the minimum public addressing requirement?
o: Two public IP addresses, one inbound and one outbound
One public IP address per device
No public address is required at all
One public IP address for the whole network, with private addresses used internally
questions.e: Only one public IP address is needed to access the Internet, while private IP addresses are used inside the private network. NAT performs the translation between the private and public addresses in both directions.
